articles.title: Banks Are Banning AI Agents Over Security... And Competition Concerns
articles.text:
Banks are banning AI agents over security... and competition concerns
AI agents are set to automate everyday banking tasks — but banks aren’t ready to give up control of the customer relationship just yet.
Banks in the United Kingdom have drawn a line over how much access artificial intelligence should have to their customers’ money.
Four banks, including HSBC, Barclays, Lloyds, NatWest and Nationwide, have all moved to block or restrict third-party AI agents from accessing customer accounts, especially where they can make transactions without customer involvement.
There’s no evidence yet of AI agents accessing UK bank accounts just yet, but large lenders are worried about what happens if an automated system mismanages customers’ money — and who would be on the hook.
The banks might have other, unspoken concerns too.
Edgars Nemše, chief executive of GenLayer Foundation, an AI-focused blockchain infrastructure project, says routine banking tasks like paying bills, moving money and finding better rates could all be handed to agents.
Unfortunately for banks, this means agents would be able to seamlessly find customers a better deal elsewhere as soon as it’s published on the web.
“For plain accounts, that removes the switching costs and makes the space even more competitive,” Nemše tells Magazine.
The risk of agentic bank runs
That scenario could threaten more than just customer loyalty. In September, Apollo chief economist Torsten Slok warned about a possible “agentic bank run.”
If swarms of agents start moving household cash from low-yield checking accounts to alternatives offering higher returns en masse, that would drain banks of the low-cost funding they rely on to make loans. And the speed and scale “would be a problem for the entire financial system.”
Related: Coinbase CEO touts agentic finance as Base tops 100M AI payments
JPMorgan Chase chief executive Jamie Dimon has also warned against allowing external agents unrestricted access to bank accounts. “You don’t want rogue agents,” he said on an October earnings call.
Is an agentic bank run coming? Source: Apollo
Regardless of short-term moves to hold back the tide, AI agents look more and more likely to revolutionize banking within a few years.
Neeraj Makin, group head of strategy analytics at Emirates NBD, predicts agents will usher in a new era of around-the-clock banking and near-instant payments as normal by 2036.
“Forget about waiting for a payment for 24 hours or inter-country payments taking three days… all of that will be in seconds, atomic,” he says, with AI agents taking over most financial decisions.
Banks risk losing the everyday customer interface
Ferdinand Dabitz, chief executive of Augustus, an AI-native banking and payments company, sees a similar shift in how customers interact with financial institutions.
“Every consumer will have 10s and every business will have 100s of agents talking to their bank,” Dabitz says.
A human interface will still remain important for managing those agents and providing a layer of trust, “especially in commercial banking,” he says.
Related: Agents can trade 24/7 — but Yat Siu warns you could lose access at any time
Emirates NBD’s developer experience team argued in July that financial institutions should build their own frameworks for agentic AI, rather than allowing individual teams to develop agents without common controls.
Its Leap framework is designed to govern how agents authenticate with core banking systems, access sensitive data and carry out actions, with audit trails, monitoring and human oversight built in.
Emirates NBD says banks should build their own agentic frameworks. Source: Emirates NBD
However there are still major concerns around the reliability of agents to make major financial decisions on their own.
A recent Bank of England and FCA survey found that while 80% of responding firms had deployed AI agents, just 2% used agents with broad autonomy, identifying data security, third-party dependencies and risks like hallucinations among their biggest concerns.
From paying bills to making financial decisions
The AI takeover likely won’t happen overnight; “it will come in steps,” Nemše says.
“Today I use an agent to review my own and my company’s finances every month and queue the payments, and I approve them. The next step is the natural one: once you trust it, you let it spend small amounts without asking.”
Routine bills, subscriptions and the agent’s own running costs would be among the first tasks to become autonomous, he says.
Dabitz says corporate treasury management could be an area delegated to agents, but says banks will need to be involved in developing these early applications.
Who pays when an agent gets it wrong?
While consumers may enjoy the upside of automating their finances, who’s on the hook when an agent makes a mistake?
Nemše says banks need to offer “delegated access as a normal feature” to avoid customers sharing logins with agents. Customers could set permissions and spending limits, and agents could make low-value transactions independently while requiring approval for larger amounts.
But existing dispute processes may struggle if agents begin making thousands of transactions on behalf of each customer. “Even a small share going wrong is a lot of disputes,” he says. “The processes for handling them were built for people making a few payments a week. That part still has to be built.”
The US Office of the Comptroller of the Currency issued a supervisory framework for banks’ use of what it calls “super intelligence,” including agentic systems, on Nov. 4.
OCC’s Super Intelligence: Supervisory Framework. Source: OCC
The framework is meant to help bank examiners assess how institutions use the technology, and does not introduce new binding requirements for banks. Scrutiny should reflect the potential consequences of an agent’s actions, its level of autonomy and the degree of human oversight.
So an AI system helping a bank employee draft a report would present a different risk from one authorized to move customer funds without approval, and the banks that get that balance right are likely to come out on top.

articles.title: Trump Backs Jensen Huang’s Return to Nvidia as Sam Altman Says 'Heroes Have Flaws' - Decrypt
articles.text:
In brief
- Trump said he would not mind Huang being reinstated, echoing Elon Musk and an online petition.
- OpenAI’s Sam Altman called Huang a hero and expressed empathy, but declined to endorse his return.
- Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent favors an outsider as Nvidia faces export scrutiny and reports earnings Tuesday.
President Donald Trump joined Elon Musk on Monday in supporting Jensen Huang’s return as Nvidia CEO, while OpenAI chief Sam Altman expressed empathy for the ousted co-founder without endorsing his reinstatement.
“I would certainly not mind seeing that,” Trump told reporters Monday as he left the White House for Asia, according to Reuters. “He could return. There’s a big group of people that would like him to return.”
Trump said Huang had “learned a big lesson,” and questioned claims that Alice Huang was a Chinese spy. “Nobody’s proven that she’s a spy,” he said, per The Guardian.
Trump also dismissed concerns that his ties with Huang threatened national security and defended Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick amid questions over enforcement of AI-chip export controls.
Musk also said Friday he was signing a petition demanding Huang’s reinstatement.
“A petition is underway to reinstate Jensen and I’m signing it too,” Musk wrote on X. Epic Games boss Tim Sweeney and Replit CEO Amjad Masad are also listed among the supporters.
More than 182,000 people had signed the open letter by Monday. It seeks Huang’s return during an independent investigation, although signatories’ identities and affiliations are not independently verified.
Altman sees echoes of his own ouster
Speaking at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World conference Monday, Altman said Huang had “long been a hero of mine. Heroes have flaws.” He described feeling “personal strong empathy” for the former Nvidia boss.
He has reason to understand a boardroom revolt. OpenAI fired Altman in November 2023, only to reinstate him less than five days later after employee and investor backlash. Still, asked whether Huang should return, Altman said: “I don’t think I know enough to answer that question.”
Altman said he struggled to imagine Nvidia without Huang, but argued the giant chipmaker was big enough to retain investor trust. That is sympathy—not an endorsement.
The fight over Nvidia’s future
Huang, who founded Nvidia in 1993, stepped down Thursday after admitting infidelity. Reports later linked him to Alice Huang and two Nvidia employees, one a subordinate.
Alice Huang previously worked at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based Nvidia customer facing scrutiny over possible diversion of advanced chips to China. Megaspeed denies wrongdoing; espionage allegations remain unproven.
Washington is tightening export controls on advanced AI chips, including new licensing requirements for shipments to Singapore and Malaysia, as officials seek to prevent diversion to China.
Trump’s backing also puts him at odds with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who said Sunday that Nvidia should look outside its ranks for a replacement. “They need a dramatic shake-up,” Bessent told Fox News.
Nvidia’s board has made no decision to reinstate Huang. CFO Colette Kress is serving as interim CEO, while the Financial Times reports Huang’s allies are lobbying for his return and Arm CEO Rene Haas is a potential successor.
Employees have also pushed for reinstatement. An internal discussion drew more than 1,600 comments, including calls for Huang’s return.
Nvidia shares opened 2.7% lower Monday, wiping out roughly $100 billion in market value at the open.
Huang could face congressional questions on China chip exports in early December. Nvidia reports earnings Tuesday, its first financial update under Kress.

articles.title: Fed Is Modeling AI 'Super Intelligence' Scenarios, Including Job Losses and a Stock Market Slump - Decrypt
articles.text:
In brief
- Warsh said Fed economists are modeling how AI “super intelligence” might affect economic growth and employment, but stressed that the scenarios are not forecasts.
- One outcome brings stronger growth and broad gains for workers; another delivers growth alongside higher unemployment as automation replaces jobs.
- The third envisions disappointing AI returns, falling stock valuations and an economic slowdown that could also pressure riskier assets such as crypto.
Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh said Monday that central bank staff have started modeling how artificial intelligence could reshape the U.S. economy, including scenarios where the technology raises unemployment even as the economy grows.
Speaking at the Fed's Productivity and Jobs conference in San Francisco, Warsh described three possible paths: a productivity boom benefiting workers, a boom that leaves workers behind, and an AI investment bust that drags down stocks and economic growth.
“These are illustrative scenarios, not forecasts,” Warsh said, explaining that staff are using simplified economic models to test what might happen over the next several years. The Fed is preparing for different outcomes, not predicting which one will materialize.
Warsh called the technology “super intelligence,” or SI. That language is now official Fed terminology after an October change following a Donald Trump administration executive order, rather than a scientific determination that today's AI systems have already surpassed human intelligence.
Three possible futures for AI
In the most optimistic scenario, AI helps companies produce more with the same resources, raising the country's economic output above its historical growth rate. Workers share in those gains, and unemployment stays close to the level economists associate with a healthy job market.
In the second scenario, AI still makes the economy grow faster, but businesses automate jobs more quickly than displaced workers can find new ones. Unemployment rises despite the productivity gains.
The third scenario assumes AI investments fail to deliver the returns Wall Street expects. Companies spend heavily on infrastructure, stock prices rise on expectations of huge profits, and those expectations eventually prove too optimistic.
“Equity valuations could fall, leading to an economic slowdown,” Warsh said. In that scenario, unemployment rises more sharply, and the economy eventually recovers without the promised productivity boost.
Those risks are already receiving attention elsewhere at the Fed. Governor Michael Barr warned Monday that the AI construction boom is increasingly financed through complex arrangements, including long-term computing leases, energy contracts and financial guarantees.
The Fed estimates that the potential maximum value of these off-balance-sheet obligations now exceeds $3 trillion. Those commitments are not the same as debt already owed, but they show why disappointing AI revenues could create problems beyond the technology companies building data centers.
Warsh did not propose an interest-rate change in Monday's remarks. The Fed's next policy meeting is scheduled for December 8 and 9.

articles.title: Strategy Buys $33M in Bitcoin, Repurchases $228M in STRC
articles.text:
Strategy buys $33M in Bitcoin, spends $228M on STRC buybacks
Strategy bought 485 Bitcoin for $33.4 million and spent $228.1 million repurchasing STRC preferred shares, largely funded by new common stock sales.
Michael Saylor’s Strategy bought 485 Bitcoin for $33.4 million last week while spending nearly seven times as much repurchasing STRC preferred shares.
The company purchased the Bitcoin (BTC) at an average price of $68,887 between Monday and Sunday, bringing its holdings to 850,849 BTC, according to a Monday filing with the US Securities and Exchange Commission.
Strategy said it raised $244.7 million by selling 2.09 million common shares (MSTR), using $33.4 million to buy Bitcoin, $206.3 million to fund STRC repurchases and $5 million to its separate cash balance. It funded the remaining $21.8 million in buybacks with interest earned on its cash and short-term investments.
The company repurchased 2.28 million STRC shares during the week. STRC is Strategy’s variable-rate preferred stock, which pays regular dividends to shareholders.
Strategy reported a $4.75 billion US dollar reserve after using $18.9 million to pay preferred stock dividends. Its separate cash balance stood at $151.2 million as of Sunday.
The company also maintained STRC’s annual dividend rate at 12% for December, saying it intends to keep the rate steady until the shares demonstrate sustained trading near $100.
Strategy spent $188.3 million repurchasing STRC shares and $81.9 million buying Bitcoin the previous week.
Strategy’s MSTR stock fell 8.45% to $102.2 in Monday’s premarket trading, while STRC declined 0.78% to $99.1, according to Yahoo Finance. The losses followed MSCI’s confirmation last week that it would remove Strategy from its global equity indexes after the Nov. 30 market close.
Related: Strategy stock sheds 5% amid MSCI index removal, Bitcoin sell-off

articles.title: Nvidia Stock Has a 20% Rebound in Sight—If Bulls Can Clear a Hurdle - Decrypt
articles.text:
In brief
- Nvidia bounced near $152.62 last week but now faces resistance around $164.40.
- The 50-week EMA remains above the 200-week EMA, although momentum indicators still favor sellers.
- Tuesday's earnings and speculation about Jensen Huang's return could decide the stock's next move.
If you were looking to buy Nvidia stock at a discount, last week may have been the best time to shop. Shares tanked following the Jensen Huang scandal involving an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, falling as low as $148.80.
On that drop, Nvidia shares touched a major support and then bounced after dropping 38% from its all-time high.
But if you didn’t buy the bottom, the second best time may be this week. The stock is trading at around $159, already up 8% from the lowest point last week. For traders relying on reading the charts, the current price of NVDA is running into another level that could decide whether the recovery has legs.
At around $159 on Monday, its weekly chart now places the $164.40 zone directly in the bulls' way.
That level previously acted as support, a price where buyers stepped in. After the breakdown, it is turning into a level to watch as investors who bought earlier may look to sell once they get their money back. But it could mark a bounce point based on the longer timeframes—as it has for at least three times since September 2025.
If Nvidia can reclaim $165 and hold above it, the next prominent resistance on the chart sits around $188 to $190. That would represent almost 20% upside from Monday's $159 price, although only about 16% from the breakout level, with possible selling pressure along the way.
Failure to clear $164.40 would put $152.62 back on the radar. Another break below that yellow support would weaken the case that last week's bounce marked a bottom.
The exponential moving averages, or EMAs, still offer some encouragement. Nvidia's 50-week EMA remains above its 200-week EMA, a bullish long-term configuration that gives more weight to recent prices but hasn't yet flipped bearish.
The shorter-term signals look less friendly. The Average Directional Index, or ADX, is around 23, suggesting a weakened trend (which is natural after the FUD episode). Its directional readings favor sellers. ADX measures trend strength, not direction by itself.
The Relative Strength Index, or RSI, is near 31.6, barely above the conventional oversold threshold of 30. That can make a relief bounce more plausible, but oversold stocks can keep falling. Neither indicator confirms a reversal yet.
Strong business, complicated leadership
Nvidia's underlying business hasn't suddenly stopped growing. The chipmaker reported $96.2 billion in quarterly revenue in August, up 106% year over year, including $89 billion from its data center business.
Investors will also be watching profit margins and the enormous financing commitments tying Nvidia to the wider AI infrastructure boom.
Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang resigned on November 12 amid reports of extramarital affairs involving Alice Huang, a businesswoman U.S. intelligence suspects of spying for China, and Nvidia executive Kimberly Powell. Reuters subsequently reported a third alleged relationship with another employee.
Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress is serving as interim CEO while an independent investigation into possible foreign-intelligence targeting continues. The espionage allegations have not been established by an independent investigation, much less in court, but were powerful enough to oust the man who led Nvidia for 33 years in record time.
The Financial Times reported that Huang has spoken with allies about returning, while a petition calling for his reinstatement has attracted more than 178,000 signatures, including Elon Musk. The board has not announced plans to bring him back.
The argument sounds familiar: Huang may be too important to Nvidia to keep out. Sam Altman returned to OpenAI days after being ousted in 2023.
Other cases of CEOs too big to let go have been Steve Jobs with Apple, Jack Dorsey with Twitter and Starbuck’s Howard Schultz. Many of these leaders have turned into the face of their companies, making it hard for the markets to trust in any successor.
For bulls, $164.40 remains the line to beat, and charts point to this outcome being quite possible. Assuming, of course, Nvidia's next big reveal is about chips and not a fourth love affair.

articles.title: Binance Pay Later Offers Up to 1,000 USDC in Crypto-Backed Credit
articles.text:
Binance Pay Later offers credit backed by Bitcoin, Ether and BNB holdings
Eligible users can access up to 1,000 USDC in credit against their Bitcoin, Ether or BNB for purchases via Binance Card or QR Pay.
Binance said Monday it would offer eligible users in Argentina and Mexico up to 1,000 USDC in spending credit through Pay Later, a payment feature backed by their cryptocurrency holdings.
Pay Later allows eligible users to access up to 1,000 USDC (USDC) in spending power against their Bitcoin (BTC), Ether (ETH) and BNB (BNB) token holdings as collateral, without selling the underlying assets, Binance said in an announcement shared with Cointelegraph. Borrowing is limited to 50% of the eligible collateral’s value, meaning $2,000 in BTC is required to access a maximum $1,000 credit line.
Purchases are interest-free until the repayment deadline on the first of the following month. Binance’s published FAQ lists a one-day grace period and interest of 0.1% per day, compounding daily, on overdue balances.
Borrowing lets users make purchases without first selling their crypto, but falling prices can put those holdings at risk. Binance can liquidate collateral when the outstanding loan reaches 90% of its value, even before repayment is due. It will initially launch for users in Argentina and Mexico, with a gradual rollout planned for additional markets.
“Traditional consumer credit often relies on income documentation and credit history, which leaves people who hold assets but have no formal credit file with fewer options,” said Thomas Gregory, VP of payments and fiat at Binance, adding that asset-backed credit offers an alternative.
Related: Securitize agrees to buy River One to expand into asset-backed lending

articles.title: Uniswap freezes $300,000 in stranded fees, halting automatic token burns
articles.text:
Quick Take
- Uniswap Labs disclosed that X Layer fees accrued without corresponding UNI burns because the installed token-bridge route rejected UNI.
- A proposed declining threshold aims to reduce the first searcher’s surplus when accumulated fees can be released.
- Proposed auction settings differ from the forum timeline, and the implementation package still appeared as a draft on Nov. 15.
Uniswap’s proposed repair for fees stranded on the X Layer network would change both the bridge used to burn UNI and the payment traders make to claim the backlog.
Uniswap Labs disclosed on Nov. 6 that protocol fees had been accruing on X Layer but could not be released, leaving the corresponding UNI unburned. Implementation reviews on Nov. 13-14 describe a higher initial UNI payment designed to reduce the windfall available to the first trader who clears that backlog.
Uniswap’s fee system relies on outside traders, known as searchers, supplying UNI in exchange for selected fee assets held in a TokenJar, a contract that collects those assets.
The payment goes toward burning UNI, and the searcher keeps the recoverable asset value above its UNI payment and execution costs.
Converting accrued fees into a completed UNI burn requires a searcher to execute the exchange and the bridge to settle it. The searcher’s net surplus is a separate return, so a release does not require Uniswap itself to buy UNI on the open market at that moment.
X Layer's governance messages use the OP Stack bridge, while token transfers use Agglayer. According to Labs, the installed relayer followed the usual OP Stack token-bridging pattern, but X Layer’s version rejects ERC-20 transfers, including UNI.
Proposal 95 records execution on March 8, including X Layer fee-activation actions. The proposed replacement would use X Layer’s token-transfer route to complete the burn.
The currently edited description of Uniswap protocol-fees implementation PR 167, opened Nov. 2, estimates that roughly $300,000 of fees could be swept into the jar. It warns that restarting with the existing 2,000 UNI payment could hand the accumulated assets to the first searcher at that fixed price.
Uniswap’s collection architecture requires explicit collection calls for v3 and v4 fees, so a jar’s wallet balance alone doesn't capture everything accrued in pools.
Uniswap's proposed auction changes the payment
PR 167 describes an initial threshold of 80,000 UNI, a 2,000 UNI floor and a two-day half-life. Its description estimates about 10.8 days to reach the floor.
The mechanism starts with an expensive claim and reduces the required payment over time. A searcher can act when the assets it can recover justify that payment and its costs, so competition could direct more backlog value into UNI payments instead of leaving the margin created by a low fixed threshold.
The proposed schedule remains inconsistent across the published plans: the Nov. 6 forum post says roughly six days after execution, while the reviewed implementation describes about 10.8 days.
Governance would start the decay after the TokenJar points to the new releaser. Anyone could update the threshold, and searchers could bundle that update with a release.
The setter would temporarily own the releaser, returning ownership and threshold-setting control to governance on the first update at the floor. The reviewed design removes a separate reclaim function, so elapsed time alone would not restore control.
As of Nov. 15, PR 169’s combined implementation remained a draft, listing the setter and replacement releaser deployment as blockers. The releaser and setter PRs remained open, while the official deployment registry still listed X Layer’s original releaser.
For scale, Strata Terminal reported $7.8 million in UNI burns over the preceding 30 days as of Nov. 15, and 14.1 million UNI in recurring burns overall, separate from the one-time 100 million UNI treasury burn.
That recurring flow gives the proposed one-time release context, but the older $300,000 backlog estimate uses a different observation date and valuation method. A direct conversion ratio would conflate an estimated stock of fees with realized burn flows.
The proposed repair’s economic test is how much UNI the release payment ultimately sends to Ethereum’s burn address.

articles.title: Saylor’s Strategy Keeps Buying Bitcoin, Adding 'A Little Orange' Through the Dip - Decrypt
articles.text:
In brief
- Strategy added 485 BTC and repurchased $228 million of its STRC preferred stock, lifting its total holdings to 850,849 BTC and $4.9 billion in USD assets as of Nov. 15, per a filing.
- The small buy paired with a sizable buyback reflects Strategy’s shift toward capital management—accumulating while defending its stock—amid a sharp Bitcoin downturn that Saylor met with a cheeky “this dip could use a little orange.”
- It lands as index provider MSCI finalizes rules that will eject Bitcoin treasury firms like Strategy from major equity indexes.
Strategy kept buying Bitcoin through a brutal market stretch, adding 485 BTC worth roughly $33.4 million and repurchasing $228 million of its preferred stock, as chairman Michael Saylor urged the market to rally with a characteristically cheeky nudge.
The company disclosed the purchase in a filing Monday. The modest addition, small by the standards of a firm that once bought tens of thousands of coins at a time, lifted Strategy’s total holdings to 850,849 BTC as of Nov. 15, alongside $4.9 billion in U.S. dollar assets.
Strategy, the largest corporate holder of Bitcoin, remains far ahead of any other treasury company.
Will Strategy hold over 1M BTC before 2027?
The buy caps a stretch of smaller, steadier accumulation paired with stock buybacks. Strategy recently added $82 million in Bitcoin while repurchasing $188 million of its STRC preferred shares, part of a shift toward what it calls a capital-management approach, buying back stock when it views the shares as undervalued rather than relentlessly stacking coins.
Bitcoin has slid sharply in recent days, trading well below the six-figure highs it touched earlier in the cycle, and the downturn has squeezed Bitcoin treasury firms whose valuations rise and fall with the asset.
Saylor, undeterred, posted the holdings update to X alongside the firm’s trademark Bitcoin tracker, and followed it with a quip aimed at the slumping market: “This dip could use a little orange,” a nod to Bitcoin’s signature color.
The purchase lands during a precarious moment for the treasury-company model Strategy pioneered. Index provider MSCI has finalized rules that could eject Bitcoin treasury firms like Strategy from its widely tracked equity indexes, classifying companies whose balance sheets are dominated by a single asset as “non-operating” and therefore ineligible.
Removal would force index-tracking funds to sell the affected shares, potentially pressuring prices and shrinking the premium these firms have long commanded over the value of their Bitcoin.
For now, Strategy is doing what it has always done, buying Bitcoin and talking it up, even as the market tests its conviction.
The combination of a small purchase and a sizable buyback underscores the balancing act: keep accumulating, defend the stock, and weather a downturn that has turned the once-unstoppable treasury trade into a far more fraught proposition.

articles.title: HKMA, Swift Explore Tokenized Deposits for Cross-Border Payments
articles.text:
HKMA, Swift explore tokenized deposits for cross-border bank payments
HKMA and Swift will explore linking Project Ensemble with Swift’s ledger for cross-border payments using tokenized deposits in multiple currencies.
The Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) and Swift will explore connecting their payment infrastructure to support cross-border transfers using tokenized bank deposits, the authority said Monday.
The work will examine links between Swift’s blockchain-based ledger and the settlement infrastructure of Project Ensemble. Participating banks include Bank of China (Hong Kong), Standard Chartered Bank (Hong Kong) and HSBC, according to the announcement.
Tokenized deposits are bank balances represented on a blockchain. They remain claims on the issuing commercial bank, unlike central bank digital currencies, which are claims on a central bank. The proposed Swift connection would explore how separate payment systems could work together across borders in multiple currencies.
The collaboration follows a Nov. 2 upgrade to EnsembleTX, the pilot phase of Project Ensemble, enabling banks to settle tokenized deposit transactions around the clock using tokenized central bank money. The pilot launched in November 2025 and initially relied on Hong Kong’s dollar-denominated real-time gross settlement system.
In July, Swift said its blockchain-based ledger was ready for initial use and that it was preparing to pilot tokenized cross-border payments with 17 major banks, including Citi, DBS and HSBC.
Related: DBS, JPMorgan’s Kinexys launch 24/7 transfers of tokenized deposits

articles.title: Ethereum test exposes flaw that lets transactions skip payments
articles.text:
Quick Take
- Developer-published Juicebox V6 simulations report four paths where transactions succeed while internal payments fail under tested Glamsterdam rules.
- The sampled mainnet comparison shows transaction failures or complete delivery across those paths, with no skipped-payment band reported.
- Ethereum's Nov. 16 testing agenda includes Juicebox's findings, while the Foundation's earlier guidance lists Nov. 19 for further discussion.
Tests of Ethereum's proposed Glamsterdam upgrade show that a transaction can succeed while a payment inside it fails, according to developer-published simulations of Juicebox V6's project-payment contracts.
Four tested paths produced that outcome in the developer's simulations on the Sepolia test network, giving core developers concrete examples of how the changes could alter application payment guarantees.
The Nov. 14 runs examine Juicebox V6 contracts that route payments between projects. Their published results include a buyer keeping an NFT while its associated payment to another project fails, and a cash-out completing while a 2.5% fee is forgiven.
A successful Ethereum receipt can miss a payment
The developer mejango says the tests use deployed contract code through eth_simulateV1. A fresh project is launched and funded inside each simulation, then a payment path is tested across different transaction gas limits. Each scenario is pinned to a blockchain block.
The V6 payout test reports successful transactions that skip a split to another project, leaving that money in the paying project. A reserved-token distribution also completes despite a failed cross-project payment, with the beneficiary receiving raw tokens instead.
In the cash-out test, sampled gas limits in the reported 679,622-to-817,622 band let the withdrawal complete without paying the fee.
The mainnet comparison runs show only transaction failures or complete delivery across the sampled ranges for all four paths.
The distinction comes from which operation runs out of gas first, according to the developer's explanation. Under the tested Glamsterdam rules, an internal payment that writes fresh storage can fail before the outer transaction does.
The contract's try/catch error handling absorbs that failure and lets the surrounding operation finish.
EIP-8037 proposes higher costs for creating persistent blockchain data and separate accounting for state creation and execution, while EIP-8038 updates the costs of accessing and writing state. Those changes aim to support more throughput while controlling resource demands.
Ethereum's Nov. 16 testing-call agenda explicitly lists Juicebox's compatibility concerns and proofs of concept within the EIP-8037/8038 investigations. The findings are intended to inform Thursday's execution-layer discussion.
In a Nov. 13 comment on that agenda, mejango asked whether the impacts fall within the Ethereum Foundation's tolerance for breaking changes, linking the answer to confidence in building immutable applications whose deployed code cannot be changed in place.
The tests advance the broader compatibility warning from early November, with specific payment outcomes from deployed contract code. They leave developers weighing whether proposed protocol rules preserve the guarantees those applications were built to deliver.
In its earlier Nov. 9 update, the Foundation recommended reviewing public audit findings before deciding on specification changes or the Hoodi testnet schedule. It lists Nov. 19 for discussion of findings and possible next steps, with no decision precommitted.

articles.title: 'Tokenization Is Not the Finish Line': Jupiter to Let Users Borrow Against Bullish Shares - Decrypt
articles.text:
In brief
- Jupiter will launch a permissioned market on Jupiter Lend where users can borrow against tokenized shares of crypto exchange Bullish, with more issuers to follow.
- COO Kash Dhanda said most tokenized assets sit idle, with only about $3.4 billion of an estimated $460 billion in tokenized assets used in DeFi.
- Jupiter also launched a Global Passport for verified identity and a liquidity service to help issuers get their tokens trading onchain.
Jupiter, the largest trading platform on Solana, is bringing Bullish's shares onchain as collateral, as part of a push to put tokenized assets to work.
The company will launch a dedicated, permissioned market on its lending platform, Jupiter Lend, starting with Bullish's NYSE-listed BLSH stock, Jupiter tweeted on Monday. More issuer tokens will follow, though the market won't be available in all jurisdictions, it added.
BREAKING:
A NYSE-listed company is bringing its own shares directly to Jupiter Lend.
Today at Breakpoint, we announced our partnership with @Bullish to launch a dedicated, permissioned $BLSH market.
For the first time, Issuer Tokens can be used as collateral inside Solana’s… pic.twitter.com/rWWqwOcWmK
— Jupiter (@JupiterExchange) November 16, 2026
Unlike many tokenized stocks, which give holders a claim on a share, Bullish's issuer-sponsored token "is itself the share," Jupiter COO Kash Dhanda said in a presentation at Solana's Breakpoint conference in London.
Users will be able to borrow against them with fully onchain liquidations in an "institutional-grade lending market," and integrations with qualified custodians, he said. Bullish acquired Equiniti, one of the world's largest transfer agents, earlier this year, Dhanda noted.
The 'utilization gap'
Dhanda framed the announcements around what he called the "post-tokenization era." Most tokenized assets today are "parked, not productive," he said.
Of the roughly $460 billion in tokenized assets tracked by data platform RWA.xyz, only about $39.5 billion is actually onchain and can be moved off the issuer's platform, and just $3.4 billion is used in DeFi, according to DeFiLlama, Dhanda said, a "utilization gap" of 99%.
"There is this myth, and this is the thing that's misunderstood: 'If you put it on chain, they will come'," he said. "This is not the field of dreams," he added, arguing that, "Tokenization is not the finish line. It is actually the starting line."
Access, trading and credit
Jupiter launched two other products alongside the Bullish market. The Jupiter Global Passport lets users verify their identity to buy permissioned assets, while keeping their information as private as possible using zero-knowledge data sharing, Dhanda said. It is live with KYC verification, with onchain credit scores and proof of wealth to follow, and the company is exploring licenses in different jurisdictions.
Will HYPE flip SOL in 2026?
Jupiter Liquidity Services, meanwhile, will help asset issuers design their markets, seed initial capital, find market makers and integrate with Jupiter's routing so that their tokens are available across the platforms that use it. "You integrate once, you will be available everywhere," Dhanda said.
"Shallow credit markets don't drive liquidity on chain," he added. "If you cannot do more with your onchain asset than you can do with the off-chain version of it, you're probably not going to switch."
Jupiter says it has handled more than $500 billion in trading volume so far this year and paid out $162 million in yield. The Breakpoint announcements follow the company's launch last week of token baskets, yield vaults and a rebuilt portfolio, and come as other venues bring tokenized stocks to Solana. Trading platform Formation has notified the SEC of plans to trade tokenized U.S. stocks on the network.
Disclosure
Jupiter powers token swaps on The Information Exchange, Decrypt's trading platform.

articles.title: Louisiana blocks prediction markets and threatens $370M in revenue from exchanges
articles.text:
Quick Take
- Louisiana’s Nov. 12 order reaches brokerage, clearing and settlement alongside exchanges, according to the CFTC complaint.
- Robinhood’s quarterly event-contract revenue and Coinbase’s annualized milestone show scale while measuring different periods.
- Changing exchanges alone offers no demonstrated protection for a broker covered by the order.
Louisiana's Nov. 12 order related to prediction markets reaches the brokers and clearing firms behind the apps, as well as the exchanges themselves.
Its scope, documented in the CFTC's federal complaint, exposes a shared legal risk for platforms earning income from different kinds of trading.
Robinhood and Coinbase each report prediction-market revenue alongside their crypto businesses. Louisiana's action reaches several layers of the trading chain, including the intermediary serving the customer.
According to the CFTC's complaint, Louisiana obtained an ex parte temporary restraining order on Nov. 12 against entities including registered exchanges, futures commission merchants and derivatives clearing organizations. Ex parte means the initial order was obtained without the other side being heard.
The complaint quotes restrictions on offering, clearing, settling, brokering and otherwise facilitating specified event contracts involving people located in Louisiana without the required state license and permit.
Its description includes sports, elections, and award events within the order's stated statutory scope.
The court-filed copy of the order names Robinhood Derivatives and Coinbase Financial Markets, along with multiple Kalshi entities, ForecastEx and Rothera.
Robinhood's product disclosure identifies Robinhood Derivatives as the intermediary and lists KalshiEX, ForecastEx, Rothera, and Crypto.com Derivatives North America as venues. Coinbase says it offers its contracts through Coinbase Financial Markets and has Kalshi operate them, which determines outcomes.
Robinhood already has several exchange routes. If the same restricted broker remains involved, moving a contract to another venue leaves the intermediary within the order's documented reach. That conditional legal-scope analysis leaves each company's implementation unconfirmed.
Prediction markets present revenue diversification and access risk
Robinhood reported $173 million in event-contract revenue for the quarter ended Sept. 30, more than six times the year-earlier figure. Cryptocurrency revenue was $120 million, down 55%.
Coinbase's Oct. 29 announcement said prediction markets had surpassed $200 million in annualized revenue.
The US and CFTC sued Louisiana and state officials on Nov. 13, arguing that federal derivatives law preempts the state's enforcement. They seek declaratory and injunctive relief, including a bar on enforcing or extending the state order.
The government's motion for a temporary restraining order and preliminary injunction is listed for submission Nov. 17. In Louisiana's enforcement case, which moved to federal court, Robinhood seeks to vacate the state order, and Rothera seeks its dissolution or modification.
In a separate federal case, Kalshi's Nov. 13 oral request concerned withdrawal of its own temporary-restraint application, with its preliminary-injunction hearing scheduled for Nov. 23.
Louisiana-specific treatment of new orders, existing positions, settlement and withdrawals remains unconfirmed.
Prediction markets can add income beyond crypto trading while leaving competing platforms exposed to the same state restrictions. A different exchange partner alone offers no demonstrated protection where the order also reaches the broker.

articles.title: Singapore, German Central Banks Advance Cross-Border Settlement via CBDCs
articles.text:
Singapore, Germany test cross-border FX settlement with CBDCs
Project Simbolon aims to reduce the cost and time of cross-border settlement and promote common standards for payments and FX
The Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) and the Deutsche Bundesbank used wholesale central bank digital currencies (CBDCs) to test settlement of euro–Singapore dollar trades across their separate digital asset test environments.
As part of Project Simbolon, the two central banks used payment-versus-payment settlement, meaning the final transfers of each currency depended on the final transfer of the other, MAS said in a Monday press release. Zero-knowledge proofs allowed each system to verify whether settlement conditions were met without directly integrating the central bank ledgers.
The project aims to make cross-border transfers between Singapore and Germany faster and cheaper. It also aims to promote common standards for cross-border payments, foreign exchange and securities transactions tied to tokenized assets.
The test was the first milestone under a November 2025 memorandum of understanding between the two central banks on tokenization and cross-border settlement. It also advances broader efforts to make tokenized financial markets more efficient under Project Guardian, a tokenization initiative MAS launched in May 2022.
“Project Simbolon paves the way for eliminating settlement risk in global foreign exchange transactions,” said Sabine Mauderer, first deputy governor of the Bundesbank.
In September, the Eurosystem launched Pontes, a system that lets financial institutions settle wholesale tokenized asset transactions in central bank money.
Related: DBS, JPMorgan’s Kinexys launch 24/7 transfers of tokenized deposits

articles.title: Solana Drops 'Mainnet Beta' After Six Years: Here's What 1.0 Is All About - Decrypt
articles.text:
In brief
- Solana has retired the “mainnet beta” label it used since March 2020 and adopted Solana 1.0 as a shared protocol version.
- The change helps Agave and Firedancer operators track network compatibility, but it does not activate new features or alter user balances.
- Solana points to the Alpenglow consensus upgrade and Firedancer's deployment as signs of maturity; neither was introduced by the renaming.
Solana is officially out of beta, more than six years after launching a blockchain that has been handling real money the whole time.
The Solana Foundation on Monday retired the “mainnet beta” label and introduced Solana 1.0, a shared version number for the network's underlying rules. The change is primarily about how developers and validator operators coordinate software updates, not a fresh boost to transaction speed or any other meaningful improvement over what users already have.
Solana launched its mainnet beta on March 16, 2020, and kept the experimental-sounding name even as users traded tokens, built applications, and moved assets across the chain.
Nothing happens to those assets now. “Your SOL, accounts, assets, applications, and transaction history remain the same,” the Foundation said. Users don't need to swap tokens, move wallets or install anything to keep using the network.
Solana has two major validator clients: Agave, developed by Anza, and Firedancer, built independently by Jump Crypto. Each has its own code, release schedule and version numbers, which can make it harder to tell whether different software releases support the same network features.
Solana 1.0 creates a common reference point for the protocol itself. An Agave release and a Firedancer release can support the same protocol version without sharing a software version number.
That distinction matters as the network relies on more than one software implementation. A bug in one client need not affect every validator, although software diversity alone cannot guarantee the network will stay online.
“Announcing a protocol version does not activate every associated improvement at once,” the Foundation warned. Operators still need to check whether their particular software supports a planned upgrade and follow its activation instructions.
The Foundation said it coordinated the change with Anza and the Firedancer team. Its announcement does not describe a new voting system or a change in who governs Solana; the network's governance process for proposals remains separate.
Why retire beta now?
The Foundation credits engineering work that preceded Monday's announcement, particularly Alpenglow and Firedancer. Solana's Alpenglow upgrade went live on October 21, replacing the system validators had used to reach agreement since launch.
Alpenglow targets transaction finality of roughly 150 milliseconds, compared with about 12.8 seconds previously. Finality is the point at which a transaction is considered settled; that improvement came from the October upgrade, not from calling the network 1.0.
Firedancer also reached mainnet in 2025, giving validators a separately developed alternative to Agave. That reduces dependence on a single codebase, though the extent of the protection depends on how widely different clients are actually used.
Solana has reasons to be careful with promises of reliability. Its network went offline for nearly five hours in February 2024, following an outage lasting almost 19 hours a year earlier.
Documentation and block explorers will gradually adopt the new mainnet name, according to the Foundation. Its upgrade tracker still lists Agave 4.4 as planned for November and Agave 4.5 for December, each with its own release and activation requirements.

articles.title: Aave’s revenue falls $10M in Q3, but one metric tells a new story
articles.text:
Quick Take
- Aave Labs reported a 40% Q3 rise in supplied assets, while its quarterly borrow-interest revenue line fell 23%.
- Lower combined SVR and liquidation receipts account for 39% of the Labs report’s quarterly revenue decline.
- Monthly revenue improved through Q3, while a separate official dashboard showed rising net income and different revenue totals.
Aave’s deposits grew during the third quarter of 2026, but the lending protocol’s quarterly borrow-interest revenue remained below the second-quarter levels, according to an Aave Labs report published Nov. 13.
The report puts supplied assets up about 40% between July 1 and Oct. 1, while its borrow-interest revenue line fell roughly 23% from the previous quarter.
Lower liquidation-related receipts explain about 39% of the overall revenue decline, but a smaller borrow-interest line also contributed substantially. Monthly revenue improved through the third quarter, and Aave’s separate official dashboard shows net income rising, so the figures do not establish a fall in profit.
What drove Aave's revenue decline
The report lists total protocol revenue of roughly $27.3 million in the second quarter and $17.3 million in the third quarter, a decline of almost $10 million (36.6%). Its named borrow-interest line fell from $16.2 million to $12.5 million, a reduction of $3.7 million.
Combining ordinary liquidation fees with Smart Value Recapture (SVR) liquidation fees gives $4.3 million in the second quarter against about $402,429 in the third quarter. That $3.9 million reduction accounts for 39.1% of the total revenue decrease.
The borrow-interest line explains another 37.1% of the decrease. Other revenue lines, net of increases, account for the remaining 23.8%. Staking income fell from nearly $1.3 million to zero, special income from about $684,000 to zero, and the separate aToken interest line declined by roughly $708,000.
Swap fees and several other interest and yield lines increased, partially offsetting those declines. The report lists GHO interest and borrow-interest accruals separately from the borrow-interest line behind the 23% comparison.
Labs reports monthly protocol revenue of $5.4 million in July, $5.7 million in August and $6.2 million in September. Its borrow-interest line also rose each month, from $3.9 million to $4.1 million, then to $4.4 million.
Meanwhile, the report’s all-version supplied balance rose from $24.1 billion on July 1 to $33.8 billion on Oct. 1. Borrowed assets increased from $10.2 billion to $13.3 billion.
Asset-price changes can affect dollar balances, so without a matching average lending balance, the tables cannot establish that Aave earned less per dollar lent. They show an endpoint balance rebound alongside a smaller quarterly revenue total.
Revenue is not profit
TokenLogic's Aave Insights dashboard reports revenue for the second and third quarters of $23.4 million and $17.8 million, respectively, different from the Labs report.
It shows net income rising from $197,930 to $1.7 million as expenses fell from $23.2 million to $16.1 million. The sources provide no numerical reconciliation between the two revenue series.
DefiLlama’s monthly revenue figures total approximately $21.3 million for April through June and $13.4 million for July through September.
DefiLlama’s methodology separates borrower fees, revenue retained by the protocol, supplier income, and tokenholder revenue. These measures cannot be substituted for Aave Labs’ profit, DAO net income or returns to AAVE holders.
Labs describes its operational figures as unaudited and subject to revision, and says they are not financial statements of Aave Labs or the DAO. The breakdown above uses that report’s revenue series throughout.
A separate development is TokenLogic’s Nov. 12 reserve-factor proposal, which changes the reserve factor across 54 asset reserves in 12 Aave V3 markets and the older V2 Ethereum market, projecting about $3.5 million in additional annualized DAO revenue at Nov. 9 balances and rates.
The proposal would lift the blended reserve factor from 12.0% to 12.7%. Its Plasma USDT0 component remains conditional on finalized terms, and the forum post lists community feedback and escalation to an on-chain proposal as next steps.
The reserve factor allocates borrower interest between suppliers and the DAO, but retaining a larger share is a different mechanism from attracting more deposits.

articles.title: DTCC, Barclays Say Tokenization's Real Prize Is Unlocking Idle Collateral - Decrypt
articles.text:
In brief
- Executives from DTCC and Barclays said the biggest near-term payoff from tokenization lies in putting collateral to work around the clock.
- Barclays' head of digital assets said much of the early value lies in moving collateral between banks' own accounts, before extending it to clients.
- Both executives said adoption is still early, but that institutions have moved from asking questions to putting real money into building.
The biggest payoff from tokenizing traditional assets won't come from simply putting them onchain, but from putting idle collateral to work, according to executives at the Depository Trust & Clearing Corporation (DTCC) and Barclays.
"You can tokenize an asset, but if you can't do anything with it, what's the point?" Val Wooton, DTCC's global head of equities solutions, said at Solana's Breakpoint conference in London. "For me, it really is around collateral and liquidity."
Scott Lucas, head of digital assets at Barclays, agreed. A lot of collateral sits "relatively idle" at central securities depositories, he said, and much of the early value for banks will come from moving it more efficiently between their own accounts, before extending that to clients. "There's a lot of money in good housekeeping," he added.
The pair spoke on a panel days after DTCC announced that its tokenization service will connect to Solana, with tokenized assets expected on the network in the second half of 2027.
The service, which launched on October 28, can tokenize assets held at DTCC's depository, starting with Russell 1000 stocks, ETFs tracking major indexes, and U.S. Treasury bills and bonds, Wooton said. The tokens carry the same legal and economic rights as traditionally held securities, and adding Solana reflects DTCC's strategy of being "open," "interoperable" and "multi-network," he added.
From 'just in case' to 'just in time'
Wooton said the biggest opportunity lies in "liquidity optimization," which he said could save "millions, if not billions" of dollars by letting firms move assets that are currently stuck when markets are closed.
Large financial institutions today over-fund and over-collateralize every day because they treat collateral as "just in case," he said. Moving assets onchain, around the clock, would let firms manage collateral "just in time," freeing up "a significant amount of balance sheet" to put to other uses. He added that the ability to move assets and settle them atomically could be "extremely powerful" in times of market stress.
Will HYPE flip SOL in 2026?
Lucas pointed to Barclays' participation in DTCC's tokenization launch last month, one of the bank's first public moves into the space, and described the efficiency gains from managing its own collateral as good housekeeping.
Barclays is also working with Ironlight on tokenized structured products, Lucas said, though he stressed "it's not a done deal." He added that he would like to see Solana adopted by other central securities depositories around the world, building a shared infrastructure layer across Asia-Pacific, Europe and the United States.
'Still in the crawl stage'
Both executives said adoption remains early. Wooton said the industry is "still in the crawl stage," and that traditional and digital rails will exist side by side "for quite a long time," though DTCC's clients are already tokenizing assets daily.
Lucas said he tries to stay "healthily skeptical" about the speed of adoption while making sure Barclays is ready for its clients. At a recent traditional finance conference in Miami, he said, "every institution we met had money on the table," making investments and building products, a shift from a year earlier, when most were still asking questions.
Barclays has been gradually expanding its crypto activities. The bank invested in U.S. stablecoin startup Ubyx earlier this year and has reportedly weighed a push into tokenized deposits and stablecoin payments, according to Bloomberg. It was also among the investors backing crypto custodian Copper in 2022.

articles.title: Bitcoin Price Rebounds From Sub-$62,000 Low Ahead of Nvidia Earnings
articles.text:
BTC price tags 18-week low into Nvidia earnings: Three things to know in Bitcoin this week
Bitcoin traders awaited Nvidia Q3 earnings after BTC price selling pressure saw a dip below $62,000 at the weekend.
Bitcoin (BTC) traded around $64,500 early Monday after a sell-off in thin weekend trading sent it to a four-month low of $61,950.
Key points:
- Bitcoin fell below its 200-week simple moving average, now at $68,186.
- Nvidia reports third-quarter earnings Tuesday following Jensen Huang’s resignation, with the company forecasting about $108 billion in revenue.
- Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh speaks Monday, and minutes of the Fed’s October policy meeting are due Wednesday.
Bitcoin falls below its 200-week moving average
Data from TradingView showed that BTC/USD fell to $61,950 on Bitstamp, a level last seen on July 13. The pair briefly rebounded to $66,000 before easing to around $64,500 during Monday’s Asian trading session.
BTC/USD one-hour chart. Source: Cointelegraph/TradingView
The drop pushed Bitcoin below its 200-week simple moving average (SMA) of $68,186. This cemented concerns about Bitcoin’s rebound to $87,000, which began in August, as flipping the 200-week SMA from resistance to support has been a prerequisite for previous bear-market recoveries.
“Deviating below the 200-week SMA has historically been the key to building out a Bear Market bottom formation,” crypto trader and analyst Rekt Capital said Saturday on X.
BTC/USD one-week chart with 200-week SMA. Source: Cointelegraph/TradingView
From Friday to 10 am UTC on Monday, Bitcoin open interest fell by around 9.1% to $20.98 billion, according to onchain analytics platform CryptoQuant.
A CryptoQuant contributing analyst drew comparisons to similar open interest drawdowns in February and June, considering whether Bitcoin was forming a local bottom.
“If the flush is complete, a bottoming zone may be near. If shorts keep piling up, even a modest rally could squeeze them. The $59K-$60K summer low remains the next key test,” the analyst wrote on Sunday.
Bitcoin open interest. Source: CryptoQuant
Bitcoin perpetual futures funding rates briefly turned negative near the weekend low, meaning traders with short positions paid those with long positions.
Bitcoin funding rates. Source: CryptoQuant
Nvidia earnings due Tuesday as allies push for Huang’s return
Nvidia remains in the spotlight this week as the tech giant reports third-quarter results after US markets close Tuesday amid ongoing controversy over former CEO Jensen Huang.
On Tuesday, interim CEO Colette Kress will lead the company’s earnings call. Nvidia previously forecast quarterly revenue of around $108 billion, and analysts expect earnings per share to nearly double year over year.
Huang is reportedly considering a return to Nvidia. He resigned last week after reports that he had an affair with a chip executive whom US authorities suspect of spying for China. Beijing denied the espionage allegation.
The Financial Times reported that a “war room” of tech CEOs and others was lobbying for his reinstatement, while an open letter calling for his return has garnered more than 165,000 signatories, including Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk.
“A petition is underway to reinstate Jensen and I’m signing it too,” Musk said in an X post on Friday.
The efforts face friction from US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who said that Nvidia should hire its next CEO from outside the company.
“This makes me think that as the board conducts a search for a new leader that they need to go outside the company, that just [with] what was going on inside the company, they need a dramatic shakeup,” he told Fox News.
Nvidia shares closed Friday at $162.85, down 12.7% for the week. On Thursday, shares fell to $148.80, their lowest since mid-2025, before recovering some of their losses.
Nvidia stock one-week chart. Source: Cointelegraph/TradingView
Nvidia headlines rattled tech stocks and crypto markets last week. Investors will be watching the company’s outlook for signs of how demand for AI chips is holding up.
Fed minutes due as markets price in December rate hike
Fed officials will speak throughout the week as traders look for clues about the December rate decision.
Related: Here’s what happened in crypto today
Warsh will deliver opening remarks at the Fed’s Productivity and Jobs Task Force Conference in San Francisco at 9 am PT (5 pm UTC) on Monday. He will also moderate two panels and a fireside chat.
On Wednesday, the Fed will release minutes of its Oct. 27–28 policy meeting. Officials left rates unchanged at 3.75% to 4%, and Warsh cited “resilient” domestic spending in the face of global geopolitical uncertainty.
After the latest economic data, markets fully priced in a quarter-point rate hike from the Fed in December. Last week’s Consumer Price Index (CPI) beat expectations, and while the Producer Price Index (PPI) reading was lower than anticipated, the annual increase was still the largest in four years.
Meanwhile, the 10-year US Treasury yield rose above 5%, and the Japanese yen brought back a familiar headwind for crypto markets as it weakened past the key psychological level of 160 per US dollar on Friday.
USD/JPY one-day chart. Source: Cointelegraph/TradingView
Japan’s economy shrank at an annualized rate of 0.1% in the third quarter, according to data released Monday. The contraction complicates the outlook for further rate hikes in Japan, where the policy rate is already at a three-decade high of 1.25%.
“With the yen perched precariously at 160 per dollar, a combination of sluggish domestic growth and sticky price pressures, if they were to materialize, would complicate life for both the Bank of Japan and the Ministry of Finance,” economist Mohamed El-Erian wrote over the weekend.

articles.title: Bitcoin Lightning developers patch bug that could make completed payments disappear
articles.text:
Quick Take
- Bitcoin Lightning developers patched an LND vulnerability that could cause nodes to lose track of settled payment records after restarting.
- The flaw caused a software counter to reset at 65,536 entries, potentially disrupting payment-channel accounting and the accuracy of settlement records.
- Developers identified a way peers could trigger the overflow, but whether any live nodes encountered the bug before the patch remains unknown.
Bitcoin Lightning developers patched a software vulnerability that could cause nodes to lose track of settled payments after a restart, potentially disrupting the accounting records that secure payment channels.
The flaw affected LND, a widely used implementation of Bitcoin's Lightning Network, which enables users to send Bitcoin through payment channels without recording every transaction directly on the blockchain.
Developers released v0.21.8-beta and v0.20.8-beta on Nov. 11 to address the issue, which stemmed from an error in how the software saved and restored channel updates.
The vulnerability could cause a node to reconstruct incomplete payment records after restarting, even when the original information remained stored on its disk.
That failure threatened the consistency of Lightning channels, where participants rely on accurate records to determine which payments have settled and what each party is owed.
According to LND maintainer Olaoluwa Osuntokun, known as Roasbeef, the problem involved a counter that tracked acknowledged updates from a connected Lightning peer.
The software stored the number of entries using a 16-bit unsigned integer, which can represent values only up to 65,535.
Once the list reached 65,536 entries, the counter reset to zero, even though LND continued writing the updates to storage.
Upon restarting, the node could interpret that zero as an empty list and omit a previously settled hashed timelock contract (HTLC), a conditional payment mechanism that helps secure transactions across Lightning channels.
Developers identify how Lightning peers could trigger the flaw
The vulnerability became more concerning after developers identified a potential way for connected peers to push the affected update list toward its limit.
In the GitHub discussion, LND collaborator ziggie1984 explained that a peer could repeatedly send transaction fee updates and commitment signatures while withholding a required revocation message.
That behavior allowed the list of pending acknowledgments to grow without being cleared.
The developer reproduced the behavior in a unit test, generating 201 stored updates after 200 rounds of messages.
Crucially, the accumulated entries survived reconnects, suggesting that repeatedly disconnecting and reconnecting would not necessarily prevent the list from eventually reaching the overflow threshold.
The potential weakness matters because Lightning depends on both parties maintaining consistent payment-channel states. Losing track of a settled update could undermine the records used to reconcile channel obligations.
However, the project's disclosures do not identify any confirmed exploitation or financial losses associated with the flaw.
To address the problem, developers introduced checks that prevent oversized update lists from advancing the channel state or being written to storage.
They also modified how LND reads existing records, allowing nodes to recover complete update lists saved by older versions when the underlying data passes validation.
The fix was merged into LND's main development branch on Nov. 5 before being included in both November releases.

articles.title: DBS, JPMorgan Launch 24/7 Transfers of Tokenized Deposits
articles.text:
DBS, JPMorgan’s Kinexys launch 24/7 transfers of tokenized deposits
Ant International is the first customer to use the service, which lets clients transfer US dollar deposits between Singapore and the US.
DBS and JPMorgan launched a service on Monday that lets clients transfer tokenized US dollar deposits between the two banks around the clock.
Tokenized deposits are bank deposits represented on the blockchain. The service connects DBS Token Services with JPMorgan’s Kinexys platform for transfers between Singapore and the US, according to a press release.
Ant International became the first client to use service to manage its cash across markets.
The launch supports the Monetary Authority of Singapore’s Project BLOOM, which aims to make it easier to use tokenized deposits and regulated stablecoins for payments in Singapore and across borders. The central bank launched the project in October 2025.
DBS and JPMorgan co-lead Project BLOOM’s working group on transfers between blockchain platforms. The two banks first revealed plans to develop a blockchain-based tokenization framework for onchain transfers in November 2025.
More than half of the 422 business leaders DBS surveyed across 11 markets said their companies used tokenized deposits or planned to do so, according to the bank’s Oct. 28 report.
Related: Citi, DBS complete first weekend tokenized cross-border deposit on Swift

articles.title: 'Nobody Knows Who's in Charge': Boris Johnson Stands by Bitcoin Skepticism at Breakpoint - Decrypt
articles.text:
In brief
- Former UK Prime Minister Boris Johnson told Solana's Breakpoint conference in London that he remains skeptical of Bitcoin, asking who guarantees it and who is in charge.
- Johnson said his doubts don't extend to blockchain, saying London should lead in the technology and in tokenizing assets.
- Lord Ross Kempsell, a Conservative peer and former Johnson aide, said the UK's coming crypto rules leave room for a "high growth industry."
Former UK Prime Minister Boris Johnson is sticking to his doubts about Bitcoin, telling a room full of crypto developers that he still can't see who is in charge of the world's largest cryptocurrency.
"As far as I can see, nobody knows who's in charge, apart from Yakimoto Nakasori, and I don't know where to find him," Johnson said at Solana's Breakpoint conference in London, deliberately mangling the name of Bitcoin's pseudonymous creator, Satoshi Nakamoto. "If six billion got stolen from some cryptocurrency, I wouldn't know who to apply to, or how to get the money back. That's my problem."
Johnson was asked about a column he wrote in March for the Daily Mail, in which he called Bitcoin a "giant Ponzi scheme." The column drew pushback from the crypto industry, including Strategy executive chairman Michael Saylor, who tweeted that Bitcoin has no issuer, promoter or guaranteed return.
Bitcoin is not a Ponzi scheme. A Ponzi requires a central operator promising returns and paying early investors with funds from later ones. Bitcoin has no issuer, no promoter, and no guaranteed return—just an open, decentralized monetary network driven by code and market demand.
— Michael Saylor (@saylor) March 13, 2026
On stage, Johnson admitted he is "not a great crypto buff" and holds little, if any, crypto himself. His view was shaped by a man he met in his Oxfordshire village who had lost thousands and kept paying more in the hope of recovering his losses, he said. "If the search for the greater fool had reached the wilds of South Oxfordshire, then probably there was something not quite right about this thing," Johnson said.
He also questioned the name itself, noting that "crypto" comes from the Greek for "hidden." "I don't think it's a good sell to tell people that this thing is concealed," he said.
'Luddite anxiety'
Johnson drew a sharp line between Bitcoin and the technology behind it. "Please don't think that my Luddite anxiety about crypto in any way means that I wish to slow down the development of blockchain, or the lead that London should rightly have in that sort of technology," he said. When it comes to blockchain and tokenizing assets, the UK has "got to be at the forefront," he added.
Moderator Gareth Jenkinson, head of multimedia at The Block, pushed back when Johnson suggested Bitcoin was valuable to drug dealers, arguing that blockchains are far more traceable than cash. Asked by Johnson who guarantees Bitcoin, Jenkinson replied: "No one has to guarantee it. That's the beauty of the protocol."
Regulation on the way
Lord Ross Kempsell, a Conservative member of the House of Lords who previously worked for Johnson, said more than 8% of UK adults now hold some form of crypto asset, and that institutional adoption of blockchains is growing in the City of London. That ownership figure has fallen, however: the Financial Conduct Authority's latest consumer research, conducted in August and September 2025, found 8% of UK adults own crypto, down from 12% in 2024, though still double the level in 2021.
The UK is "on the precipice of creating a lot of regulation" for the sector, Kempsell said, pointing to the FCA's work on its regulatory perimeter and the Bank of England's coming stablecoin framework. "I share Boris's anxieties about the risks," he said, but within that perimeter, "there's a lot of scope here for a high growth industry."
In June, the FCA finalized its rulebook for crypto firms ahead of a mandatory regime due to take effect in late 2027, days after the Bank of England eased its stablecoin rules, scrapping planned individual holding caps in favor of a £40 billion issuance limit per coin. The Bank has since been handed a legal duty to foster stablecoin innovation, and it has set out a shared vision for tokenization with the FCA.
Kempsell also argued that being outside the EU's Markets in Crypto-Assets (MiCA) regulation allows the UK to set its own rules for crypto. The EU itself is set to revise MiCA in 2027 to cover foreign stablecoin issuers.

articles.title: Strategy planned to slow STRC buybacks near $100 but spent another $1.4 billion instead
articles.text:
Quick Take
- Strategy spent $1.4 billion repurchasing STRC at weekly average prices above $99, accounting for 52% of its $2.7 billion buyback spending.
- The heavy purchases contrast with management's July plan to scale back repurchases as STRC approached its $100 stated value.
- With just $332 million remaining, Strategy faces a decision on expanding its buyback program while Bitcoin acquisitions remain subdued.
Strategy has spent more repurchasing STRC near $100 than at deeper discounts, testing its stated strategy of slowing purchases as the preferred stock approaches face value.
A CryptoSlate analysis of the Michael Saylor-founded company's regulatory filings shows that it spent approximately $1.4 billion buying back STRC between Sept. 28 and Nov. 15, when weekly average purchase prices ranged from $99.06 to $99.93.
That represents 52% of the nearly $2.7 billion Strategy has spent under its preferred-stock repurchase program since July. By comparison, the company spent approximately $1.28 billion during the preceding 10 weeks, when its average purchase prices were below $99.
Averages are shown to two decimals by STRC.live, derived from issuer-reported share counts and buyback spending rounded to $0.1 million, so cents are approximate. The Nov. 9–15 average is calculated from Strategy’s $228.1 million and 2,282,510 shares. The $100 series is the security’s stated amount.
The spending has coincided with STRC's recovery toward its $100 stated value. The preferred stock briefly touched $100 on Nov. 4 for the first time since May before retreating below that threshold.
However, the continued buying contrasts with the approach Strategy CEO Phong Le outlined in July.
Le said the company intended to scale purchases according to price and liquidity, buying “more at deeper discounts and less as the STRC trading price approaches $100 per share.”
Strategy's shrinking STRC discount raises questions over buyback strategy
The company's weekly disclosures show that its STRC spending generally increased as the discount narrowed.
Strategy initially spent $25 million repurchasing 288,930 shares at an average price of $86.52 between July 20 and July 26.
By Sept. 28-Oct. 4, weekly spending had climbed to $176.3 million at an average price of $99.39, even though the discount to stated value had narrowed from nearly 13.5% to approximately 0.6%.
Buyback spending is reported to the nearest $0.1 million. Each bar is assigned to its reporting period end date, not necessarily a calendar week. The Sep. 8–13 reporting interval contains six days. Companion chart shows average price per share.
Purchases remained substantial in subsequent weeks, reaching a record $228.1 million between Nov. 9 and Nov. 15 at an implied average price of $99.93.
The sustained spending has also made Strategy a significant participant in STRC trading.
Pro-MSTR analyst Zaid estimated that the company's latest repurchases equaled 25.2% of STRC's total weekly trading volume, describing its presence as being toward the higher end of historical buyback activity.
Meanwhile, Crypto Banter founder Ran Neuner highlighted the scale of the intervention, observing that Strategy had repurchased nearly 30% of the STRC it had issued.
The company nevertheless has an economic incentive to continue retiring shares near face value.
STRC currently carries a 12% annualized dividend, meaning repurchases reduce future dividend obligations at the prevailing rate.
However, Strategy's ability to maintain its current buying pace under the existing program is diminishing.
Its latest SEC filing showed just $332.2 million remaining under its $3 billion authorization, with nearly 89% already exhausted.
At the latest weekly pace, another $228.1 million in repurchases would leave approximately $104 million available.
Zaid suggested another expansion could arrive soon, given the spending pace. Strategy previously raised the authorization from $1 billion to $2 billion in September and to $3 billion in October.
Bitcoin purchases slow
Strategy has continued accumulating Bitcoin alongside its preferred-stock repurchases, although purchases have slowed considerably.
Between Sept. 28 and Nov. 15, the company acquired 3,183 BTC for approximately $253.1 million, compared with the $1.39 billion spent on STRC during the same period.
The gap was particularly pronounced last week, when Strategy spent $228.1 million to repurchase STRC, compared with just $33.4 million to acquire 485 BTC.
Those transactions increased its Bitcoin holdings to 850,849 BTC, acquired for approximately $64.2 billion at an average price of $75,452 per coin. The firm currently has unrealized losses of more than $10 billion.
Strategy funded $206.3 million of its latest STRC repurchases through MSTR common-stock sales, highlighting the trade-off between reducing preferred-dividend obligations and expanding its Bitcoin treasury.
That capital-allocation decision comes as the company faces another challenge.
Index provider MSCI has confirmed Strategy's removal from its global equity indexes, effective Dec. 1, under rules excluding companies classified as non-operating businesses.
The exclusion could create additional selling pressure from index-tracking funds, potentially weakening MSTR's share price and making equity-funded Bitcoin purchases less attractive.
With its STRC repurchase authorization nearly exhausted, Strategy must decide whether to expand the program again or reduce purchases near $100.
That decision will also help determine whether the company can return to the larger Bitcoin acquisitions seen earlier this year while its common stock adjusts to the loss of MSCI index membership.

articles.title: Harvard, Dartmouth Retain Bitcoin ETF Stakes Amid Q3 BTC Rally
articles.text:
Harvard, Dartmouth keep Bitcoin ETF stakes steady as fund gains 42% in Q3
Harvard’s gold ETF share count rose nearly 20-fold in Q3, while Dartmouth kept its positions in Solana and Ether staking ETFs unchanged.
Harvard University and Dartmouth College reported unchanged share counts in BlackRock’s spot Bitcoin exchange-traded fund (ETF) at the end of the third quarter as a Bitcoin rally lifted the value of both stakes.
Harvard held 3.04 million shares of the iShares Bitcoin Trust ETF (IBIT), worth about $144.1 million at the end of September, while Dartmouth reported 201,531 shares valued at $9.5 million, according to Form 13F filings with the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC).
IBIT gained about 42% in Q3 as Bitcoin (BTC) rallied nearly 43%. Both posted their strongest quarterly gains of 2026 through September.
Harvard has reported the same IBIT share count since the end of March, after cutting its holdings by 43% in Q1 and 21% in Q4 2025. Dartmouth has reported the same 201,531 shares since first disclosing its Bitcoin ETF position in Q4 2025.
Harvard increased its share count in the State Street’s SPDR Gold Shares ETF (GLD) nearly 20-fold in Q3, to 1.16 million from 58,862. The position was worth $442.2 million at the end of September.
Dartmouth again reported 304,803 shares of the Bitwise Solana Staking ETF and 178,148 shares of the Grayscale Ethereum Staking ETF. The positions were worth $4.9 million and $4.5 million, respectively, at quarter-end.
The steady university holdings contrasted with moves by major financial companies. Jane Street reduced its IBIT shares by 19% in Q3, while JPMorgan Chase increased the number of shares it held by 9.6%, according to their latest quarterly filings.
