articles.title: Jordan Belfort’s new AI voice startup, Tone, wants to sell like the 'Wolf of Wall Street' | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Years ago, as questions mounted about WeWork’s soaring valuation, I sat down with co-founder Adam Neumann. We were negotiating a stage interview, and he asked to meet me twice in the weeks leading up to it, once at a WeWork in San Francisco and again at his office in New York.
I knew full well that the numbers that SoftBank in particular had assigned to WeWork made little sense, but I came away understanding why investors wanted to throw in their lot with him.
It’s similarly easy to understand why people are enchanted by Jordan Belfort, the self-proclaimed “Wolf of Wall Street.” Belfort famously pleaded guilty in 1999 to securities fraud and money laundering tied to Stratton Oakmont, the Long Island brokerage where salespeople pushed penny stocks in pump-and-dump schemes while Belfort acquired a Southampton mansion, a 167-foot yacht, and at least one helicopter. (He destroyed the latter two while high on quaaludes and cocaine, as depicted in Martin Scorsese’s famous adaptation of Belfort’s autobiography, “The Wolf of Wall Street.”)
You might think someone who spent 22 months in prison and was ordered to pay $110.4 million in restitution to 1,513 victims wouldn’t get another shake. The victims ultimately received “far less” than they were owed, TMZ reported in July, noting that Belfort completed his court-ordered restitution obligations in late April of this year.
But Belfort, whose energy has a galvanizing quality, keeps resurfacing, including in recent years as a Miami-based sales consultant and one-time host of crypto workshops at his Miami Beach home. (A New York Times reporter attended a weekend workshop several years ago where the price of admission was one bitcoin or its equivalent value at the time of $40,000.)
Now he is moving into the intersection of what he knows best — sales — and the hottest trend on the planet, AI, building out a voice-based AI platform. The secret sauce is that it imbues its voices with the kind of tonality that wins deals, he says, for example, by phrasing declarative statements as questions (which “builds engagement”) and even whispering at times (which “implies scarcity of information”).
Belfort says the platform, called Tone, is already being used by companies that have more sales leads than their human teams can handle. Now, in a move that could also help expand its training data, Tone is launching a self-service platform for content creators and authors who want to turn their books into “expressive AI-generated narration.” Users can select from Tone’s AI voices or, as a voice-cloning feature rolls out, create a clone of their own voice.
It’s easy to argue the market is already saturated with AI voice startups and technologies, and Tone comes with added risk: Belfort’s co-founder in the business is longtime investor Shervin Pishevar, who has a controversial past of his own. We also can’t independently verify that the technology works as described (neither co-founder is an engineer).
But if my time with Neumann taught me anything, it’s that doubts about the numbers rarely get in the way of a good pitch. When Belfort looks for investors to back him in this new venture, finding believers won’t be too hard.
Here is part of our conversation, edited for length and clarity.
What have you built?
It’s a very unique way of going about building a voice, and it stems from a system of influence and persuasion I’ve been teaching since the late 1980s. It’s not just what you say, but how you say it. When you’re not in person, body language collapses into tonality. There are about 15 very powerful tonalities that people use all the time. The phrase I invented for this was “goal-oriented communication.” If I’m trying to be perceived as an expert, I apply tonality strategically.
Is this effectively trained on you?
It started that way. As a non-engineer, I went to first principles: How would I teach a human to do this? One tonality at a time. I have 30 years of super high-quality data , and I started teaching the model. It was a breakthrough moment, because it not only sounded exactly like me, it had nailed the tonality. Then I taught it a second one, and then how to link them. The key to all of this is data. Even the littlest bit of corrupt data dramatically negates the progress you’ve made.
How did you and Shervin Pishevar come together?
Shervin and I have been personal friends for a long time, and we were out for dinner one night. I had been pitched by an AI company that said it had an AI that could do selling. I listened to it. It was awful. But it put the idea in my head. I thought I was just going to teach models how to sell, but I couldn’t find a voice that was good enough. Necessity is the mother of invention, so we built our own.
Who are your customers, and how do they use it?
We have law firms and health insurance companies. We do a lot in polling and automobiles. It will take you through an entire health insurance sale. It asks qualifying questions, like what type of insurance you want, your budget, your ages. Then it chooses a plan and explains the features and benefits. Our latency is like 600 milliseconds. If the payment is too high, it’ll say it can bring the payment down and explain how to raise your deductible. If you don’t like the plan, it swaps you to a different one. It does literally the whole entire sale.
How does the AI handle a sales call that goes off script?
It never says, “That’s a great question,” unless it really is. I hate that. It’s so ingratiating. In any sale there’s a happy path, how we’d want the perfect conversation to go, and every last word can be mapped out. But people have questions and concerns, and they take you off the straight line. So the trick is a model that can carry that perfect conversation, handle anything thrown at it, answer elegantly and return to the straight line, without breaking rapport and without hallucinating — or, as a salesperson, lying. We’ve trained the model to do that.
Have you generated any revenue from Tone yet? Have you raised funding for it?
Revenue, probably about a million bucks — $700,000, maybe. We’ve raised friends and family and seed, about $10 million.
I want to address the elephant in the room. You have a fraud conviction. Pishevar has faced misconduct allegations that he denies. Why should a bank or a hospital or a consumer brand trust this product coming from the two of you?
All I can say for myself is that I did make mistakes. It was a very, very long time ago, and I’ve spent the last 20-plus years teaching people all over the world. I’ve been hired by companies all over the world to teach sales and persuasion. If some companies don’t want to work with us, that’s their decision. But I think there would be more than enough that would see the value of what we created.
What close rate does Tone have versus a typical sales force?
I still don’t think it’s quite as good as a top producer. A top producer in the field would outdo it call for call. I think that will change in the next six months to a year. To make a model respond this quickly, you’re not using frontier models. We’re using our own very small, very light models, so they don’t have quite as much intelligence. I think it will significantly outperform a mediocre closer.
Where is it used most effectively? Low-dollar sales opportunities? I’d think the more money someone is spending, the more human contact they’d demand.
I don’t think it’s about replacing humans. What I see most with customers is that they simply don’t have the human capital available. They could get a lot more leads than they have people to call, or they need coverage at different times of day or in different languages. I think there’s always going to be a need for great human salespeople. I really believe that.
You’re competing with ElevenLabs and Cartesia and a lot of other voice AI companies. Tone is your edge?
I don’t think sounding human is really what this is about. They’ll all sound human in six months or a year. It’s the application of tonality that makes us different: the intelligence behind when it chooses a certain tonality. We have a patent on it. ElevenLabs is a great company, and Cartesia as well, but those voices didn’t work for us.
The FCC ruled in 2024 that AI voices fall under robocall rules under the Telephone Consumer Protection Act. How does outbound sales calling work?
We only call opt-in. You’re not going to use AI to cold-call people. We would not allow that. You’d get sued by every TCPA lawyer in the world. It’s either opted-in leads or existing customers. The exception is polling, where there’s an exemption that lets you call private homes without opt-in.
How do you verify consent and prevent impersonation in voice cloning?
We could launch the cloning tomorrow. We didn’t. If you create a clone in our system, you speak into the computer, so we know who is creating it, and that person signs a consent. If someone wants to upload audio, which we don’t recommend, you’d have to match a live voiceprint in real time.
Who created the technology? You’re not an engineer, and Pishevar isn’t, either. I saw a name on the patent, Jordan Anthony Metzner.
No. Our VP of engineering is Ben Sussman. He’s a brilliant engineer. I’m the judge and the jury and the executioner of what sounds perfect. I’ll prototype something in the most obscene way, and my engineers rebuild it from scratch.
Do you charge per minute, or based on the outcomes customers see?
A combination. For streaming, it’s per minute. The content platform will be monthly subscriptions. And we have some clients where the bulk of our money is made through success.
Is this an independent company or something that belongs inside a larger AI company?
If the right offer came up, and it was substantial enough, and I thought it made sense, who wouldn’t entertain a conversation? But right now my plan is to raise a significant amount. I don’t think we need to own data centers, but we need enough reserve compute. I wouldn’t think I’d be selling it anytime soon, but who knows what the future brings.
Paramount+ released a documentary about you this summer. Did you watch it?
I didn’t. Believe it or not, I don’t watch or read anything about me, good or bad. I never read a comment. When you’re well-known, you have to live by who you are inside. I go by my own internal compass.

articles.title: In Get Huge, the manosphere is here to make friends — with deadly consequences
articles.text:
Before Clavicular and other manosphere streamers were introducing young guys to the concept of breaking their facial bones to become more attractive, there was an older generation of creators building massive followings with content focused on chemical biohacking. Were it not for steroid-obsessed influencers like Anthony “Tony Huge” Hughes launching YouTube channels over a decade ago, looksmaxxing might not have become such a prominent part of the digital media landscape in 2026. These creators became internet famous by presenting themselves as peak male specimens. But their larger-than-life online personas often concealed the truth about how sinister and toxic this kind of influencing can really be.
In Get Huge, the manosphere is here to make friends — with deadly consequences
Get Huge: Looksmaxxing to Death gets at the heart of how influencers are radicalizing impressionable men.
In Get Huge, the manosphere is here to make friends — with deadly consequences
Get Huge: Looksmaxxing to Death gets at the heart of how influencers are radicalizing impressionable men.
Hughes is the gravitational center of Get Huge: Looksmaxxing to Death — Hulu’s new three-part docuseries from director Stacey Lee. The series is both a deep dive into Hughes’ strange life and a fascinating exploration of how perilous the creator economy can be in the age of manosphere and looksmaxxing influencers. Through Hughes’ ever-expanding orbit of creators, Lee is able to highlight how lonely, impressionable men are all too easily radicalized by what they see and post online. And it makes clear that all these men are trapped in a deadly psychological prison of their own making.
Get Huge takes some time to touch on Hughes’ former life as a bankruptcy lawyer and supplement salesman who was investigated by the FDA for hawking unapproved performance-enhancing drugs. But most of the series takes place in Pattaya, Thailand, where Hughes spends his days producing content showcasing his extravagant life of nonstop partying and injecting substances that swell his muscles to huge proportions. Hughes takes pride in his image as a man with access to a harem of women, and the fact that his money gives him power over many of the people around him. He presents himself as the ruler of a small kingdom — and his entire brand is built on the idea that he can show people how to become more like him.
The men caught in Hughes’ aspirational fantasy aren’t just stateside fans who’ll never reach his muscle-y heights. He is also marketing himself to other established bodybuilding influencers who might be interested in joining his inner circle by following him to Thailand. These include a menagerie of biohacking / manosphere influencers who became vital parts of Hughes’ operation over the years. Leo Longevity (legal name Laith Abdallah Algaz), Elon Muscular (his legal name isn’t revealed), and Connor Murphy all built sizable social media presences of their own. But they were each compelled to move to Pattaya and join Hughes’ entourage by a powerful desire to feel connected to something larger and more fulfilling than their individual followings.
As Get Huge features clips of Hughes’ videos — the bulk of which are now only featured on Rumble and X following multiple account bans on YouTube and TikTok — you can see that he’s trying to sell his audience on his highly specific way of life. Hughes’ own videos make it seem like he’s living his dream surrounded by people who revere him. But with each interview, Get Huge makes it clear that for all of his posturing, Hughes has been living in something of a nightmare — one where many of his disciples have died under mysterious circumstances.
As these men explain why they were drawn to Hughes, you get the sense that looksmaxxing culture is a direct response to the widespread disaffection that followed the last decade of interconnected societal shifts, from the #MeToo movement to Donald Trump’s presidencies. Hughes seems very much like an entrepreneur profiting from men’s loneliness by convincing them that their lives would be better if they were part of his community. As Get Huge first maps out Hughes’ friendships, they all appear to be anchored by an odd, sometimes envious, but genuine kind of intimacy. But as the documentary digs deeper into its subjects’ lives, it becomes hard to see them as anything but emotionally stunted men who perform cartoonish masculinity for one another in ways that are psychologically unhealthy and, at times, physically dangerous.
Part of what makes Get Huge such an unsettling watch is how relatively calm and collected Hughes and the other interviewees are as they begin to discuss how many people in their circle have died in recent years. Hughes and Murphy grow closer as friends following Algaz’s death in 2023, but they seem to bond by making Algaz the butt of the joke in content produced after his death. Simply by letting these men speak frankly about their social dynamics, Get Huge reveals the manosphere as a space in which connections built on mogging and the objectification of women can quickly deteriorate into infighting and petty jealousy. Elon Muscular readily speculates that Murphy might have had something to do with Algaz’s death because Murphy openly jokes about it. And the entire situation becomes that much stranger and more grim when Get Huge reveals that Murphy drowned shortly after the series initially wrapped filming.
Though the deaths in Hughes’ circle bring a dark whodunit energy to Get Huge, the documentary emphasizes how much peril comes as a part of existing in the looksmaxxing space. Rather than trying to solve the mystery of how Algaz died, the docuseries presents his story as a cautionary tale. He’s an object lesson in how this lifestyle can warp a person’s perception of reality in a way that ultimately cuts them off from the kind of help they really need.
What might be most disturbing about Get Huge is the way it ends. The series follows Hughes to a youth bodybuilding event where he talks up his less-than-legal products to a new group of boys — some as young as 13. To keep his momentum going, Hughes has to appeal to a new, younger audience that doesn’t understand how everything about looksmaxxing is a performance. Though the docuseries gives you the distinct impression that people like Murphy and Algaz felt a true belonging with Hughes, its closing shots call into question how genuine any of his connections with other bodybuilders really are. By juxtaposing the deaths of Hughes’ adult acolytes with his focus on turning children into fans, Get Huge paints a clear picture of how the manosphere’s promise of emotional connection often ends in a twisted kind of exploitation. And that extractive energy feels foundational to a culture that runs on people turning every aspect of their lives into content.
All three episodes of Get Huge: Looksmaxxing to Death are now streaming on Hulu and Disney Plus.

articles.title: Chase blames a software bug for Monday’s US online banking outages
articles.text:
JPMorgan Chase blamed a software bug in its own on-premise hardware for Monday’s online banking problems at several big US banks. The bank said in a post on X that there was no evidence of a cyberattack. It aims to fix the issue by the end of the day.
JPMorganChase has experienced a temporary issue related to a software bug in on-premise hardware systems – there is no evidence this is cyber-related. It is taking longer than usual to service some customers.
Where we were party to a transaction involving other banks, those banks may have been impacted, but this is not a systemic issue.
Customers still have access to their accounts and funds.
We’re working diligently to resolve this by the end of the day today.
— Chase (@Chase) November 16, 2026
Other banks felt it only where they were party to a transaction with Chase, the bank said, and “this is not a systemic issue.” Its customers still have access to their accounts and funds.
Thousands of reports
Reports about Chase on Downdetector peaked at nearly 5,000 around 2pm ET, Forbes reported. Customers of Bank of America, Wells Fargo, U.S. Bank and Zelle also logged problems, in smaller numbers.
Of the Chase reports, 52% concerned balances and transactions, 21% web log-ins and 17% transfers, The Hill found. Chase’s app told customers that some services were not available.
Some Chase customers said on social media they could not use ATM cards or finish transactions in branches. The New York Times reported those posts.
Other banks and Zelle
The problems centred on Chase customers and on people at other banks trying to transact with Chase, the Associated Press reported. Bank of America and Citigroup had no problems with their own services, according to the AP.
“U.S. Bank systems are not directly impacted. However, clients attempting to send or receive Zelle payments with another financial institution may experience transaction delays,” U.S. Bank said in a statement.
Zelle, which a group of banks owns through Early Warning Services, said its network was working.
“An issue at the financial institutions may be impacting broader services, including Zelle payments, for some of their customers,” a Zelle spokesperson said.
The Federal Reserve’s own payment systems, including ACH transfers between banks, kept working normally. ABC News reported that from the Fed’s website.
A third outage in five days
The banking problems followed Microsoft’s Outlook outage, which began on Thursday. Microsoft called that a technical issue, unrelated to cyberattacks or AI agents.
On Friday, the FAA ordered a nationwide ground stop after its air traffic communications network failed. Officials traced it to an Arkansas router upgrade. The FAA said it was not a cybersecurity incident either.
There was no indication the bank problems were related to Microsoft’s outage, The New York Times reported.

articles.title: Google adds 66 regional dialects to Gemini - Engadget
articles.text:
Google adds 66 regional dialects to Gemini
The feature was teased during Google I/O earlier this year.
One of the less visible risks of conversational AI is its flattening effect on a culture's unique dialect and accent. Humanity speaks with a thousand voices, but assistants often just respond in a nicely generic transatlantic monotone. Now, Google is doing something about it by adding 66 regional dialects to Gemini to help it better relate to the people using it. The feature was first teased at Google I/O earlier this year, and starting today, the Android and iOS apps will be able to speak to users in a variety of voices from different countries.
For instance, UK users can set Gemini to speak in a Geordie, Scouse and Brummie accent to better engage with people from Tyneside, Merseyside and Birmingham. The list also includes Scots, Welsh, Northern Irish and Multicultural London English, among many others. And it's not just the UK that gets this treatment, with tailored dialects for India, Brazil, Indonesia and Korea also in the mix.
Google says it worked with native speakers to ensure the voices were authentic and clear, rather than exaggerated and stereotypical. It added that Gemini isn't going to suddenly fill its responses with "street slang," but instead focus on sounding more "like a local." Given how much pride people put into their accent as a signifier of their heritage, it'll be very interesting to see how well these voices are received by the people intended to use them.
To activate the voices, you'll need to access the voice settings in the Gemini app or tap the three-dot menu. Google suggests a good way to test their authenticity is to ask for a recommendation for local food to better hear the "warmth and rhythm of each voice."

articles.title: Lãi suất ngân hàng hôm nay 16/11/2026: Giảm lãi suất 3 kỳ hạn, gửi 24 tháng còn 6,9%/năm
articles.text:
Lãi suất huy động liên tục được các ngân hàng điều chỉnh giảm kể từ sau khi NHNN ban hành Văn bản số 9608/NHNN-CSTT ngày 18/10/2026 về việc triển khai các giải pháp về hoạt động của các tổ chức tín dụng.
Hầu hết các ngân hàng đều đã thực hiện giảm lãi suất sau chỉ đạo trên, trong đó có ngân hàng đã có từ 2-3 lần thực hiện điều chỉnh lãi suất huy động sau chỉ đạo của NHNN.
Trong số đó, Ngân hàng TMCP Việt Nam Thịnh Vượng (VPBank) vừa có lần thứ ba liên tiếp giảm lãi suất huy động với mức giảm từ 0,2-0,3 điểm phần trăm lãi suất các kỳ hạn 15, 18, 24 tháng.
Theo đó, lãi suất tiết kiệm kỳ hạn 15-18 tháng được VPBank điều chỉnh giảm 0,3 điểm phần trăm; lãi suất tiết kiệm kỳ hạn 24 tháng giảm 0,2 điểm phần trăm. Lãi suất các kỳ hạn còn lại không thay đổi.
Với mức giảm của lãi suất như trên, lãi suất tiền gửi trực tuyến lĩnh lãi cuối kỳ được VPBank áp dụng cho tài khoản tiền gửi dưới 10 tỷ đồng gồm: Kỳ hạn 1-5 tháng 4,65%/năm, kỳ hạn 6-11 tháng 6,6%/năm, kỳ hạn 12-13 tháng 6,7%/năm, kỳ hạn 15-18 tháng 7,1%/năm, kỳ hạn 24 tháng 6,9%/năm, kỳ hạn 36 tháng 6%/năm.
Lãi suất ngân hàng áp dụng cho tài khoản tiền gửi từ 10 tỷ đồng trở lên có sự khác biệt ở các kỳ hạn từ 6-13 tháng. Theo đó, lãi suất ngân hàng niêm yết như sau: Kỳ hạn 6-11 tháng 6,8%/năm, kỳ hạn 12-13 tháng 6,9%/năm, trong khi lãi suất ngân hàng niêm yết cho các kỳ hạn còn lại không thay đổi so với tài khoản tiền gửi dưới 10 tỷ đồng.
Trước đó, VPBank từng giảm 0,1 điểm phần trăm lãi suất tiền gửi kỳ hạn 1-5 tháng vào đầu tháng 11 và giảm 0,4 điểm phần trăm lãi suất các kỳ hạn 6-13 tháng trong tháng 10.
Với việc vừa tiếp tục điều chỉnh lãi suất, VPBank là ngân hàng thứ 5 cùng với TPBank, OCB, Techcombank và Eximbank đã có hơn một lần công bố giảm lãi suất huy động kể từ sau ngày 18/10.

articles.title: AO3 Is Back. This Is Not a Drill
articles.text:
Dust off that Hitachi and put your Slack on “Do not disturb,” because AO3 is back online, baby.
After weeks off the internet due to an unspecified security incident, the Organization for Transformative Works (OTW), the nonprofit that runs the hugely popular fan fiction forum, announced on November 15 that service had been restored.
“We understand that the wait and uncertainty surrounding AO3’s return have been difficult, and we apologize for the inconvenience,” the statement reads. “We greatly appreciate your support during the downtime, and continued patience as our volunteers work hard to return AO3 to its full functionality.”
The news came as a pleasant surprise to AO3’s devoted fans, as the website had announced in late October that restoring service could take between two to four weeks. To that end, the OTW statement says that some of the site’s features, such as user icons and external work importing, have been temporarily disabled in order to expedite the site’s return. It also warned that users “may experience a delay before AO3 loads,” due to “high traffic.”
Founded in 2007, AO3 is one of the most popular fan fiction forums on the internet, boasting more than 11 million users and over 18 million original works. Following its temporary shutdown, many devastated fans started sharing Google Docs of their favorite fanfics, sparking some concerns among authors worried about AI scraping and their work being posted to other websites without their permission. Others resorted to other platforms to get their Dramione or Hollanov fix, such as Tumblr, which reported a 75 percent jump in new sign-ups among users between the ages of 18 and 25, according to data shared with WIRED.
Throughout the 17-day shutdown, AO3 has remained vague about the causes of the security breach. In its statement announcing its return, OTW said that while it has “no reason to believe that the user database was compromised,” it can’t rule out the possibility; the website recommends users change their passwords “as a precaution.” The site is also pairing with a security firm “to help prevent future incidents.”
Though the suggestion prompted some concern on social media, for the most part fans are jubilant about the end of the “AO3 apocalypse,” as some have referred to the shutdown.
“Ao3 returned on a Sunday,” one fan wrote in a tweet that has 1.2 million views. “Just like Jesus.”

articles.title: OpenAI will embed safety researchers to investigate AI subversion | TechCrunch
articles.text:
OpenAI will embed safety evaluators from Apollo Research, Goodfire, METR, and Transluce in its organization as part of a pilot, OpenAI said Monday. The news follows a series of safety incidents, including one in which an OpenAI agent swarm broke out of its sandbox and hacked into Hugging Face during cybersecurity testing. Many AI safety researchers, including from Apollo, have argued such an event might have been avoided if outside evaluators had been embedded within OpenAI to monitor its safety testing.
OpenAI said the efforts support its commitments to rely on independent assessments of safety controls under the White House Accord on Super Intelligence. The pilots will begin at different points, with Apollo’s beginning this week, according to OpenAI.
The idea of embedding evaluators into frontier AI labs first came from Anthropic, which last month started to give METR researchers employee-level access to its systems. Until recently, AI companies have only brought in outside reviewers to test models after post-training and shortly before public release. Evaluators say this is insufficient because it doesn’t allow them to test for misaligned behaviors like scheming during training or to monitor internal deployment use cases that could still pose a threat.
The work with each third-party firm differs in scope. The pilot with OpenAI and Apollo will focus on investigating whether models attempt to subvert their own or their successors’ alignment or control mechanisms. In other words, they’ll be on the lookout for whether AI models try to undermine the safety rules and safeguards designed to keep them, or future versions of themselves, under human control. OpenAI recently published findings that while training GPT-5.6 Sol, it began leaving instructions for future versions of itself telling them to conceal mistakes and misaligned behavior from the user.
Per Apollo, the pilot will examine whether training incentivizes subversion; whether evaluations can elicit subversion; whether subversion occurs during internal deployment; and whether reasoning relevant to subversion would be detectable. These risks are becoming increasingly important to monitor as AI models grow more capable of acting autonomously and deceiving humans. Apollo’s previous research with OpenAI found that models can behave differently when they know they’re being tested and tend to prioritize what evaluators want to see over users’ actual institutions.
Goodfire will embed researchers who specialize in understanding how AI models work internally. Using its interpretability platform, the firm will help OpenAI monitor training runs, fix undesired behavior, and improve alignment, per the company. Goodfire says it will publish findings, though its primary audience will be OpenAI’s own researchers.
With METR, OpenAI plans to perform two evaluations: one that looks for unintended or dangerous behavior in the model itself, including problems OpenAI’s own tests might have missed, and another that tests whether OpenAI’s systems are capable of catching that behavior. For the first evaluation, METR will largely decide for itself what to investigate and how to test the model. OpenAI and METR have not yet come to a decision on the scope of the second assessment, according to OpenAI.
Transluce, meanwhile, will examine whether OpenAI’s post-training safety evaluations themselves are good enough. The organization is also planning to test in 2027 how OpenAI uses its safety tests to decide whether a model is safe enough to release.
At a time when the independence of third-party evaluations is under scrutiny, it’s worth noting that Apollo and Goodfire are both receiving financial compensation for their evaluations. METR and Transluce aren’t, but they may accept compute or API credits.
Apollo, which published the most detailed account of its agreement with OpenAI, offers a closer look at the scope and limitations of these evaluations.
Many in the AI safety community have warned that AI labs might try to stymy evaluators’ independence, especially if outsiders find unflattering evidence that labs would rather keep hidden. Apollo says an essential part of the pilot is OpenAI’s agreement that the firm can publicly explain the conditions and limitations of its work.
Still, there are areas where Apollo believes its access to OpenAI’s systems is lacking. For a truly independent evaluation of the company’s AI models, Apollo says it needs true employee-level access to OpenAI’s systems, including “all data, records and documentation relevant to their assessment even if a developer was trying to hide unfavorable information.” Getting access to all data, including training data and evaluation logs which companies are loathe to show to outsiders, is important for, say, checking a company’s claims about how a model performed or determining when certain concerning behavior emerged.
In previous coverage, John Steidley, chief of staff at Palisade Research, told TechCrunch that it’s important to see this data in order to assess whether a model was trained to perform well on a “shutdown resistance benchmark.”
In OpenAI’s first pilot, the AI lab is providing Apollo with access to only the information required to assess whether the models engage in subversion attempts. This includes “relevant training code and datasets, reinforcement-learning rollouts with available reasoning traces and rewards, and the ability to query intermediate model checkpoints.”
The scope of access will be limited to “only the agreed claims and only for the specific models and time periods agreed for the assessment,” Apollo says. OpenAI still reserves the right to withhold certain information within that scope if it deems it necessary because of technical infeasibility, security risks, or IP protection. The company agreed not to withhold information simply because it is unfavorable.
Apollo also won’t get access to all OpenAI staffers, instead being limited to “only authorized staff,” which are participants that the AI lab selects, though Apollo can suggest certain individuals. Crucially, if an OpenAI employee outside this group raises confidential information within the scope of Apollo’s research, the firm cannot follow up and will need to cease communication and route follow-up through OpenAI.
That condition is significant. It comes in the wake of OpenAI firing three researchers for allegedly sharing confidential information with safety evaluation firm METR — which performed the Hugging Face incident post-mortem alongside independent AI safety research group Redwood.
Buck Shlegeris, CEO of Redwood, said in a post on Monday that the agreements announced don’t meet the bar of granting third parties “employee-like access,” saying it’s “disappointing but not surprising.”
OpenAI said that they'd have embedded evaluations with employee-like access; the agreements announced today obviously don't meet that bar.
This is disappointing but not surprising.
Maybe future agreements will be better. https://t.co/kmDbg1Dqav
— Buck Shlegeris (@bshlgrs) November 16, 2026
The pilot will also be limited in how much researchers can disclose. While Apollo will be allowed to publish independent conclusions of its findings, OpenAI will be able to limit evidence available to substantiate them publicly, which could make it hard for outsiders to independently assess the findings. Apollo has pushed back against this limitation, saying it believes researchers should be allowed to disclose the findings of the evaluation “to an appropriate outside audience even if the developer was trying to prevent the disclosure of unfavorable findings.”
That said, while the public cannot see the full supporting evidence, OpenAI says its Safety and Security Committee, which oversees safety on behalf of the OpenAI Foundation’s board, will get to review unredacted assessment reports and can communicate privately with evaluators.
While OpenAI is not granting all of Apollo’s conditions for a truly independent evaluation, the firm says the pilot is “an ambitious first step towards deeper access and disclosure rights,” and that it is working toward running full embedded evaluations with multiple AI developers in the future.
This article has been updated to include pilots with METR, Goodfire, and Transluce, as well as with information from OpenAI and comment from Redwood.

articles.title: Tổng Bí thư, Chủ tịch nước Tô Lâm cùng lãnh đạo Pháp, Campuchia thăm gian hàng Viettel Campuchia tại FrancoTech 2026
articles.text:
Trong khuôn khổ Diễn đàn Công nghệ và Đổi mới sáng tạo Pháp ngữ FrancoTech 2026 tại Phnom Penh, Tổng Bí thư, Chủ tịch nước Tô Lâm cùng Tổng thống Pháp Emmanuel Macron, Thủ tướng Campuchia Hun Manet và đoàn đại biểu cấp cao đã đến tham quan gian hàng Viettel Campuchia (Metfone) – đơn vị thuộc Tập đoàn Công nghiệp – Viễn thông Quân đội (Viettel) đang hoạt động tại Campuchia.
Tham gia đoàn có Đại tướng Phan Văn Giang, Phó Thủ tướng, Bộ trưởng Bộ Quốc phòng Việt Nam cùng các đại biểu cấp cao. Tại gian hàng, Ban Tổng Giám đốc Viettel Campuchia đã giới thiệu với đoàn về hoạt động của doanh nghiệp, các sản phẩm công nghệ và giải pháp số đang được triển khai tại thị trường Campuchia.
Viettel Campuchia, với thương hiệu Metfone, chính thức cung cấp dịch vụ viễn thông từ năm 2009. Sau hơn 17 năm hoạt động, doanh nghiệp đã xây dựng mạng lưới viễn thông rộng khắp, cung cấp các dịch vụ kết nối cho người dân và doanh nghiệp, đồng thời từng bước mở rộng sang lĩnh vực công nghệ thông tin và dịch vụ số.
Tại FrancoTech 2026, Viettel Campuchia giới thiệu các sản phẩm và giải pháp công nghệ trong lĩnh vực viễn thông, tài chính số, y tế, giáo dục và logistics. Các giải pháp hướng đến ứng dụng công nghệ trong thực tế, từ nâng cao chất lượng kết nối, hỗ trợ giao dịch số đến cải thiện khả năng tiếp cận các dịch vụ thiết yếu, đáp ứng nhu cầu ngày càng đa dạng của người dân và doanh nghiệp Campuchia.
Việc phát triển các nền tảng và dịch vụ số tại Campuchia nằm trong định hướng mở rộng hoạt động của Viettel tại các thị trường quốc tế, từ cung cấp dịch vụ viễn thông truyền thống sang các lĩnh vực công nghệ số. Trong đó, Viettel Campuchia là một trong những đơn vị có thời gian hoạt động lâu năm, gắn liền với quá trình phát triển hạ tầng viễn thông và chuyển đổi số tại thị trường sở tại.
Hoạt động tham quan gian hàng Viettel Campuchia diễn ra trong khuôn khổ FrancoTech 2026, diễn đàn tập trung vào các xu hướng công nghệ, đổi mới sáng tạo và hợp tác giữa các doanh nghiệp, tổ chức trong cộng đồng Pháp ngữ. Được tổ chức tại Phnom Penh nhân dịp Hội nghị Cấp cao Pháp ngữ lần thứ 20, sự kiện quy tụ các doanh nghiệp công nghệ và đối tác quốc tế, tạo cơ hội giới thiệu sản phẩm, trao đổi kinh nghiệm và tìm kiếm các hướng hợp tác trong lĩnh vực chuyển đổi số.
Trong bối cảnh hợp tác kinh tế và chuyển đổi số tiếp tục là những lĩnh vực được Việt Nam và Campuchia quan tâm thúc đẩy, hoạt động của các doanh nghiệp như Viettel Campuchia góp phần mở rộng kết nối, ứng dụng công nghệ và tăng cường hợp tác giữa hai nước. Từ lĩnh vực viễn thông, doanh nghiệp đang từng bước phát triển thêm các dịch vụ số phục vụ hoạt động kinh tế – xã hội tại Campuchia./.

articles.title: Instagram will let creators add Amazon affiliate links directly to their posts and Reels - Engadget
articles.text:
Instagram will let creators add Amazon affiliate links directly to their posts and Reels
The app will become even more of a shopping mall, just in time for Black Friday.
Meta has a new gift for Instagram creators just in time for Black Friday and the holiday shopping season. The company is making it easier for influencers to promote Amazon affiliate products directly in their posts without having to rely on a link in bio service.
US creators who are also in Amazon's influencer program will now be able to add dozens of affiliate links directly to their Reels and Instagram posts, Meta announced. The links will take viewers directly to the Amazon app and creators will earn their usual commission from any purchase made via their content.
Instagram has enabled product tagging and shoppable posts for some time. But the company previously required that tagged products in Reels already exist in Meta's commerce catalog. Now, creators can instead link their Amazon account directly to Instagram and add up to 30 products in a single video (there's a 20-product limit for feed posts). The Instagram app will also show creators what commission to expect for each item.
For creators, the timing of the new feature is particularly good. Commission from affiliate links is a central part of how many Instagram influencers earn money from their accounts. And posts with products linked directly can generate twice as many clicks as bio links, according to Meta. And while the company won't take a cut of creators' commissions, these links are no doubt a valuable source of data to Meta about what their users are interested in.
The update is the latest way Meta has made it easier for Instagram influencers to direct users off-platform. The company has also started allowing creators to add clickable links to captions and Reels if they pay for certain Meta One subscription plans. Those paid tiers also come with expanded link pages. Up to now, the company's restrictions on link-sharing have led many creators to depend on separate "link in bio" services. Now, it seems Meta is increasingly interested in offering those tools to creators directly.
For now, Amazon affiliate linking is only available to creators in the United States who have a professional account on Instagram and are 18 or older. The company hasn't said if it plans to expand the feature to creators in more countries.

articles.title: ‘Loyal to your old country’: Ramaphosa on Musk and Starlink
articles.text:
Elon Musk’s difficulty with South Africa’s ownership policy is what keeps Starlink out of the country, President Cyril Ramaphosa said on Monday. He was speaking to ABC News’ Jonathan Karl at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World event in California.
“All countries have policies in terms of how they admit companies to operate. The United States has the same,” Ramaphosa said. “When you want to come and operate here, you’ve got to subscribe to the policies of the country.”
South Africa’s telecoms law sets at least 30% ownership by historically disadvantaged groups for individual licences, TechCentral reported. SpaceX has refused to give up 30% of its local operation, so Starlink’s entry has stalled.
Communications minister Solly Malatsi told Icasa in December 2025 to consider equity-equivalent investment programmes instead. In May 2026, Icasa said it could not fully apply that direction without a change to the law. On 9 November, business group Sakeliga asked the Pretoria high court to set Icasa’s decision aside, according to TechCentral.
‘He should give back’
Musk grew up in South Africa. He has called its rules “openly racist ownership laws”, in a February 2025 post on X. Karl said Musk has also accused Ramaphosa of building an apartheid 2.0.
Ramaphosa said Musk is conservative by nature and does not fully understand what apartheid did to Black South Africans. The apartheid government spent 12 rand on Musk’s education for every one rand it spent on his, Ramaphosa said.
“If one does not understand that, one will never be able to understand precisely what needs to be done to remedy the harm that was done,” he said.
Ramaphosa said there had been talk of a meeting with Musk on this trip, but their diaries had not matched. He said Musk’s brilliance had awed him in the past.
“Even as one is a citizen of a new country, you should still be loyal to your old country,” Ramaphosa said.
Musk owes what he has become to his education in South Africa, Ramaphosa added. He should give back to the country, he said. Karl also noted that Musk had been involved in the US midterms, where his candidates lost almost everywhere.
An ‘ambush’ at the White House
Ramaphosa called his Oval Office meeting with Donald Trump an ambush. Trump showed him videos there that he said were from South Africa. He said Trump was seriously misinformed, because the video and press clippings did not show South Africa.
“We are Nelson Mandela’s children and we respect the human rights of everyone. Black, white, everyone,” he said, adding that there is no white genocide in South Africa.
He said falsehoods have shaped how the US relates to South Africa. He and Trump have not spoken since that meeting.
Data centres and AI meetings
US voters have pushed back against AI data centres, and ballot measures rejected them. South Africa has had the opposite experience, Ramaphosa said. The country is home to almost 70% of the data centres built on the African continent, he said.
His biggest worry about AI is technology out of human control, he said. He raised the point at the BRICS meeting in India. He said he agreed with AI leaders who call for global guardrails, and warned against autonomous weapons making decisions.
Ramaphosa said he would hold meetings with OpenAI, Anthropic, Microsoft, and Google, and with their investors. His delegation of nearly 300 people includes ministers, South African tech firms, and students. He wants more US companies to join the 600 already operating in South Africa.

articles.title: California sues OpenAI over rogue AI hacking incidents
articles.text:
California is suing OpenAI after its AI agents broke out of their testing environment and hacked other companies, including Hugging Face. In a lawsuit filed Monday, Attorney General Rob Bonta accuses OpenAI of violating consumer safety law by knowingly developing a “dangerous product without proper oversight,” as reported earlier by Reuters.
California sues OpenAI over rogue AI hacking incidents
OpenAI lost control of its AI agents more than 80 times during testing, California’s AG claims.
The lawsuit claims the cyberattack on Hugging Face “was the predictable result of an internal culture at OpenAI that prioritizes growth and rapid model development over safety and accountability.” It alleges that OpenAI recently told the attorney general’s office that it “lost control” of its AI agents more than 80 times during testing.
After revealing the rogue AI attack on Hugging Face in July, news of several other similar incidents emerged, including attacks on an Australian government website, a German wiki site, and the software package manager RubyGems. OpenAI’s agents also tried to “bruteforce” a United Nations website.
“OpenAI’s actions escalated real-world cybersecurity risks, threatening the safety, health, and well-being of society,” Bonta says in the press release. “The company knowingly tested a dangerous product without proper oversight or safety procedures and misled the public about it — this disregard for public safety violated California law.”
OpenAI released its new cybersecurity AI model earlier this month, saying that it’s less likely to go rogue and attack other platforms. It’s also giving safety evaluators at Apollo Research access to its AI systems as part of a pilot program that monitors models for misalignment.
“Since the Hugging Face incident, we’ve undertaken an extensive and transparent effort to understand and address misaligned model activity,” OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri says in an emailed statement to The Verge. “This lawsuit appears to single out OpenAI over a challenge that’s been identified by every major AI lab. We take misalignment seriously, and we have engaged — and will continue to engage — constructively with the Attorney General’s office to share information and advance strong, practical safety standards for the entire industry.”

articles.title: SPX Express linh hoạt giao nhận, hỗ trợ nhà bán tăng tốc mùa cao điểm
articles.text:
Chủ động bàn giao hàng hóa trong mùa cao điểm
Mùa kinh doanh cuối năm thường kéo theo lượng đơn hàng tăng mạnh, tạo áp lực lên khâu chuẩn bị, bàn giao và vận chuyển. Trong bối cảnh đó, các giải pháp giao nhận linh hoạt trở thành lựa chọn giúp nhà bán tối ưu quy trình, đáp ứng tốt hơn nhu cầu của người mua.
Tại SPX, dịch vụ lấy hàng tận nơi kết hợp mạng lưới điểm gửi hàng mang đến nhiều phương án phù hợp với nhu cầu vận hành. Nếu hình thức lấy hàng tận nơi giúp tiết kiệm công sức, đặc biệt với nhà bán có lượng đơn lớn hoặc hàng hóa cồng kềnh, việc trực tiếp mang hàng đến điểm gửi giúp chủ động đưa đơn vào quy trình vận chuyển.
Từ năm 2025, SPX đã triển khai chương trình Đối tác điểm giao nhận, kết nối với các điểm giao nhận đối tác bên cạnh hệ thống bưu cục sẵn có, giúp nhà bán thuận tiện hơn khi gửi hàng trực tiếp.
“Vào mùa kinh doanh cao điểm cuối năm, đơn hàng tăng là tín hiệu đáng mừng, nên tôi cũng chú trọng lựa chọn giải pháp để đội ngũ hiện có xử lý đơn hiệu quả hơn. Từ khi có thêm lựa chọn mang hàng đến điểm gửi SPX, tôi có thể chủ động gửi những đơn đã đóng gói xong theo từng đợt, hạn chế để hàng chờ lâu tại cửa hàng.
Nhờ vậy, việc bàn giao thuận tiện hơn, nhân viên cũng bớt áp lực dồn việc và có thời gian kiểm tra hàng, chăm sóc khách chu đáo hơn. Với tôi, tăng đơn phải đi cùng với chất lượng phục vụ”, chị Thu Hà, chủ một cửa hàng thời trang tại Hà Nội chia sẻ.
Linh hoạt nhận hàng, gia tăng cơ hội hoàn tất giao dịch
Bên cạnh khâu gửi hàng, trải nghiệm nhận hàng cũng tác động trực tiếp đến quyết định mua sắm của khách hàng. Đặc biệt trong mùa mua sắm cuối năm, khi khách hàng có xu hướng đặt nhiều sản phẩm trong cùng một đơn, các lựa chọn kiểm tra hàng hoặc nhận một phần đơn hàng có thể giúp quá trình giao nhận thuận tiện hơn.
Bên cạnh các hình thức hỗ trợ kiểm tra hàng trước khi thanh toán, tính năng giao hàng một phần của SPX cho phép người mua nhận những sản phẩm phù hợp và gửi trả các sản phẩm còn lại ngay tại thời điểm giao hàng, trong phạm vi dịch vụ hỗ trợ. Với một số trường hợp đơn hàng có nhiều chi tiết hoặc sản phẩm, việc điều chỉnh danh mục hàng giao, hàng trả và số tiền thu hộ (COD) tương ứng cũng có thể được thực hiện tại điểm giao theo quy trình áp dụng, với sự phối hợp trực tiếp giữ nhân viên giao nhận và người bán.
Giải pháp này còn hỗ trợ nhà bán hạn chế việc phải xử lý lại toàn bộ đơn hàng khi người mua chỉ có nhu cầu giữ lại một số sản phẩm. Nhờ đó, quá trình giao nhận có thêm phương án xử lý phù hợp với tình huống thực tế, thay vì mặc định trả lại toàn bộ đơn.
“Nhu cầu mua sắm quần áo và đồ dùng dịp cuối năm thường tăng cao, nhưng khách hàng vẫn có những băn khoăn về kích cỡ hoặc mức độ phù hợp của sản phẩm khi nhận hàng. Với các đơn hàng đáp ứng điều kiện giao hàng một phần, khách có thể lựa chọn những món phù hợp ngay tại thời điểm giao.
Điều này giúp cửa hàng tăng cơ hội bán hàng, hạn chế việc khách trả lại toàn bộ đơn, đồng thời vẫn ghi nhận doanh thu từ những món khách chọn nhận và đáp ứng sát hơn nhu cầu thực tế của người mua”, anh Minh Quân, nhà bán hàng tiêu dùng tại TP.HCM cho biết.
Ở góc độ người tiêu dùng, những lựa chọn này góp phần giảm bớt sự bất tiện trong quá trình nhận hàng. “Tôi thường mua vài món trong cùng một đơn, nên nếu có sản phẩm chưa phù hợp thì vẫn muốn nhận những món còn lại. Việc được kiểm tra và nhận một phần đơn hàng giúp tôi tiết kiệm thời gian, không phải trả lại cả gói rồi chờ giao lại những món cần mua”, chị Khánh Linh (TP.HCM) chia sẻ.
Trong mùa mua sắm cuối năm, khả năng thích ứng với nhu cầu thực tế ở từng khâu giao nhận ngày càng trở thành một phần quan trọng trong hoạt động kinh doanh trực tuyến. Từ việc chủ động lựa chọn cách bàn giao hàng đến tạo thuận tiện cho người mua khi nhận bưu kiện, các giải pháp linh hoạt của SPX góp phần giúp nhà bán duy trì tiến độ xử lý đơn và đáp ứng tốt hơn nhu cầu khách hàng, qua đó gia tăng cơ hội hoàn tất giao dịch và tăng trưởng doanh thu.
| Trong tháng 11/2026, SPX triển khai các chương trình ưu đãi dành cho khách hàng sử dụng dịch vụ vận chuyển trên toàn quốc, bao gồm ưu đãi giảm giá lên đến 50% cho tất cả các nhà bán và chương trình giá dùng thử 11.000 đồng cho nhà bán mới. articles.title: Jensen Huang Is Gone. Now What?
articles.text:
I don’t go into any given week at WIRED assuming I’ll be thinking much about extramarital affairs. But last week, they were the only thing on my mind.
These thoughts, of course, were prompted by Jensen Huang. In the span of a few completely insane days, the billionaire CEO and cofounder of Nvidia went from being a globally influential Silicon Valley executive to a lesson in exactly what not to do if you want to keep your job, and the extraordinary power that comes with it. It’s a damn mess—for Huang and his family, sure, but also for Nvidia, the AI industry the company is instrumental in powering, and the entirety of the global economy.
WIRED’s senior correspondent Lauren Goode has spent years reporting on Nvidia and Huang, including interviewing the man himself on multiple occasions. She also spent last week breaking news about his downfall, despite being in Europe on vacation. (Sorry, Lauren. You can have those PTO days back.) So at the end of a very long week for WIRED’s newsroom, I called Lauren to talk about what she makes of Huang’s ouster, what it means for AI, and where this all goes next. We also made a bet about Huang’s future—one involving a meal he recently made semi-famous.
This interview has been edited for length and clarity.
KATIE DRUMMOND: Lauren, first of all, thank you for your tirelessness these past few days. The last time I saw you, we were both in Miami for WIRED’s big event, and you were getting on a red-eye that night to go to Europe for vacation, which didn’t exactly go as planned. When you saw that first story about Jensen’s affair on Sunday, what did you think? What went through your mind?
LAUREN GOODE: Oof. The story first started bubbling up a while ago because The New York Times, and a lot of credit is due to The New York Times here, first reported on Nvidia’s relationship, if you want to call it that, with this company Megaspeed, back in the fall of 2025.
It was a very unusual story. And for some reason it just didn’t capture the attention of people the way that more recent reporting that we and others have been doing has.
Anyone who’s sort of been paying attention to that story, or had some sources in the industry, were starting to hear things. But the fact that the affair with this person, who goes by Alice Huang, was confirmed, that’s the kind of story that always captures people’s attention in a different way.
There are few things people love to read about more than extramarital affairs, especially when they involve powerful people. The reason it wasn’t surprising to you, was it because of that previous reporting and what you had been hearing here and there? Or was there another reason that you saw that story and thought, “OK, actually some of this is not shocking to me”?
It was both. I don’t know if you remember, Katie, but in the fall of 2024 we were doing a WIRED outing, a few of us hanging out, and we started chatting about whether or not we thought a lot of the most powerful people in Silicon Valley had girlfriends or extramarital affairs or situations. Because there are some people in Silicon Valley who are actually quite open about that. I remember us talking about it at the time, and there’s part of me that always kind of assumes that there are elements of their personal lives that we’re never going to have a full window into.
Not that we were talking about Jensen that evening, but it’s always been in my mind. Then, yes, I think being on the ground in Silicon Valley, you often hear things. But a lot of times there’s a certain threshold that things have to cross in order for us as journalists to consider something reportable or something worth chasing down as reportable.
I think an important distinction is that people cheat, people have affairs all the time, Silicon Valley or otherwise.
Right.
What tips this over into newsworthiness is, A) the Chinese espionage of it all, and B) the affair with a subordinate.
You reported that Jensen’s resignation—which really, to be clear, is the board of Nvidia ousting him—probably had more to do with the alleged affair with a subordinate than this other extramarital relationship, which is tied up in espionage allegations. A source told you this. Can you explain why that affair would tip the balance for the board?
I just think it’s important to note that this doesn’t seem like it was simply a moral decision. Someone had posted on X that “I can't believe the board caved to moral pressure.” To me, this doesn’t seem like it’s a moral issue.
I think if you’re looking at the three things that could have led to serious scrutiny of Jensen Huang’s behavior, there’s: One, extramarital affairs. Two, alleged extramarital affairs with subordinates within his own company. And three, an extramarital affair with an alleged Chinese operative, which puts Jensen Huang in this position where the board and the investigators who are looking into this are trying to determine what he knew and when he knew it, and basically whether he was aware of the fact that chips were making their way into China.
This isn’t just about the fact that someone had a girlfriend outside of their marriage. I think what is still to be revealed here could in fact be very, very serious in nature.
Now, you also reported on Monday, in a fantastic scoop for WIRED, that Jensen hired a crisis comms firm a year ago. In October 2025 he hired a fixer, Risa Heller, who is very well known for working with high-profile men who are facing allegations of sexual misconduct, among other things. I’m talking about Anthony Weiner, Mario Batali, writer Jeffrey Toobin. Tell us a little bit about that story and what you found out.
I really feel like with everything else going on this week, I could have gone without ever hearing about all of those stories again.
Oh, you don’t want to hear about Anthony Weiner all the time?
No, it turns out. I had kind of forgotten that. I was like, “I think I blocked that from my memory.” And Jeff Toobin—what a throwback.
Yes.
But this firm, it’s a really interesting firm run by this woman named Risa Heller. They have offices in New York and LA, and yes, they have this reputation for dealing with a lot of sexual misconduct cases, as well as other types of corporate and personal PR needs for high-profile people.
A source had told me a while ago, and I’m not gonna timestamp it, but a while ago that it had been rumored that Jensen Huang had hired this firm. So immediately my antenna went up, and I was like, “Wait, what?”
I thought it was curious, but I didn’t know exactly what the nature of the contract was or when they had been hired, and then eventually through more reporting, I was able to get confirmation of some of the details.
What we know is that this firm, Heller, started working with Jensen Huang sometime in 2025, and ostensibly, Huang and his family had hired Heller for their own personal PR outside of Nvidia’s walls. This is because when you’re someone like Jensen Huang, you have a lot going on. You have a family office. You do a lot of work with philanthropy. You’re hosting personal events. He’s also been grooming his adult children to take over these higher profile roles within Nvidia, so some of the PR might have ostensibly been to work on creating more of a public-facing image for his kids.
We do know, though, based on more reporting, that as of October 2025, and then closer to the end of the year, Nvidia’s internal teams had been instructed to start looping this outside crisis firm, Heller, into all press inquiries, all communications related to Jensen.
That was definitely a change from the prior terms of his working relationship with Heller, and also timing-wise coincided with that first New York Times story I mentioned. I think that it was published on October 9th, 2025, and first highlighted Megaspeed and what appeared to be a very close relationship between Jensen Huang and Alice Huang.
I can’t decide if he should get his money back for hiring this crisis comms firm, because this crisis has certainly not been contained, or if the fact that this is now coming up a year later suggests that maybe they did their job quite well for a while.
Well, first of all, I don’t think he needs the money back.
I don’t know, depends on how …
… on how his assets get divided, yes. Or if maybe they won’t divorce. You know, it’s also a very Silicon Valley thing not to necessarily do that.
I also think it’s possible that Jensen himself was not totally upfront with this firm when he hired them. Or, if they knew something was up, they may not have known all of the details. So if that is the case, hypothetically, then you can’t necessarily do everything you would typically do in terms of reputation management. TL;DR, it didn’t work out so well for him in the end.
No, things are not going well for Jensen. Now, Nvidia has named an interim CEO to replace him. Surprise, surprise, to both of us and women everywhere, she’s a woman.
It’s a woman.
What do we know about Colette Kress, who is the interim CEO of Nvidia?
Well, we know that when we emailed Jensen this summer to say, “Hey, Jensen, who do you think the most powerful women in Silicon Valley are?” He didn't mention Colette. Jensen mentioned Dina Powell from Meta and Ruth Porat from Google, both really high-ranking women, presidents of those companies.
And then [SpaceX president and COO] Gwynne Shotwell, because I prompted him. But no Colette, and that struck me as interesting at the time, too, though I didn’t press him on that. And then we did end up giving Colette a nod in our big feature that we did about high-ranking women in Silicon Valley.
Colette has been with Nvidia since 2013. Prior to that, she worked at Cisco, Microsoft. She’s CFO. She’s a financial whiz. She’s the person who appears on earnings calls with him every quarter.
She actually does a lot of the speaking, because she’s a person who has really, really deep knowledge of Nvidia’s complex financials. She’s the person who gives guidance for the next quarter. She’s CFO of arguably the world’s most important company. I think it makes sense that she would be slotted into this role.
Nvidia doesn’t really have a traditional hierarchy. They don’t have a traditional chief operating officer, for example. You know, when Steve Jobs was at the end of his tenure and he was very sick, Tim Cook, who was the operations whiz at Apple for many years prior, was basically groomed to be the CEO.
Nvidia doesn’t have someone like that. So it makes sense for now that Colette is the person who would slot in, because part of Nvidia’s goal has to be, at this point, easing the stock market. I don’t know if you’ve been following, but, I mean, it’s pretty bad out there.
I would say that, against my will, I am seeing a lot about Nvidia stock not doing well. I have not looked at my 401(k). I try really hard not to because I’m a control freak, and I simply cannot control how many affairs this man is having and what impact that has on my finances.
These things, though, help paint a picture of Jensen’s character and the way he ran the company. The fact that Nvidia did not do succession planning. There was no hierarchy; he had dozens of direct reports. There was no successor waiting in the wings. What do those things combined tell us about Jensen and Nvidia?
As I understand it, Katie, even you have had to do a succession plan, right?
Yes, without revealing too many details, Condé Nast, like most normal companies, has people in senior leadership roles do succession planning. They take it really seriously. It’s an annual exercise that we do, and my understanding is that that is very par for the course at most companies, at any company, and particularly a company of Nvidia’s stature and importance on a global scale. The idea that there would not be a formal succession plan is shocking to me.
It is shocking, and it’s shocking not just from the perspective that Jensen perhaps didn’t do that or didn’t have a super well-formulated one, but that the board wouldn’t demand that. I’ve heard a few different theories floated as to why this is. One theory is that Jensen may have had a lot of the insecurities that come with being a cofounder, CEO, someone who’s been living and breathing this company, his baby, since 1993, and not necessarily wanting to stuff the ranks with people who are just as capable, if not more capable in some measures, than himself, right?
Like you don’t create an environment in which someone could theoretically replace you that easily. So that’s one theory. The other theory is that—and Jensen himself has said this, both to me and other people in interviews too—he truly believed that keeping a flat org was better for the flow of information, that once you start to create a structure that’s too hierarchical, then any kind of changes that happen in the company, any kind of new information that comes out, even in some kind of white paper, fundamentally changes the direction of the way the industry is going.
I mean, think about the way people inside the AI industry probably reacted when they first saw the famous Transformer paper in 2017 and said, “Oh my gosh, this is going to change everything.” If you’re a big, fat, bloated, slow organization, you’re probably five years behind on your AI strategy. If you’re lean at the top, you can basically say, “Let’s go. We’re going in this direction now,” and you won’t encounter a lot of barriers to doing that. So that helps explain the flat org. It doesn’t necessarily explain the lack of a succession plan.
The third theory that’s been floated to me is that maybe in some, I don’t know, alternate universe, he really did think that his children, one of his two children, who are both working within Nvidia, would one day be the inevitable successors.
You have met Jensen several times. You’ve corresponded with him, you’ve interviewed him, you published a cover story for WIRED that featured an excellent interview with him. You published an edition of our newsletter, Backchannel, at the end of last week with a little bit about this. In it you talk about one experience you had interviewing Jensen at a conference. You wrote, “Huang was domineering, evaded some of my questions, and immediately after our session concluded, did an impromptu Q&A session with a much more adoring crowd than me.” You describe him as obsessed with controlling the narrative.
Again, we’re coming back to this theme of control. I’m curious to hear a little bit more about that observation, this idea of Jensen as fixated on storytelling and the stories that were told about Nvidia and about AI.
That particular interview was July of 2024, and Nvidia had invited me to interview Jensen again at the SIGGRAPH Conference in Denver, which is this whole confab of computer graphics nerds. It’s a really fun conference.
During the preparation for it, when I got on the call with some Nvidia comms executives, Madison Huang, Jensen’s daughter, appeared on the call and she basically took the lead and said, “Here’s this cluster of slides that when you’re on stage, Jensen’s going to be referencing, and he’s gonna have a lot to say about each slide, and it would be great if you could tee him up at this point.”
And I said, “Well, wait a second. This is not a standard journalistic interview. Like, what’s going on here?” The whole thing felt very strange, but I made it clear I planned to ask him the questions I really felt I needed to ask him as a journalist. It was just very clear he did not want to answer a lot of my questions, and that he was going to just own the stage and reference his slides. I remember that he talked about how he made a little Jensen AI of himself, and the crowd was all, “Ha! Jensen AI,” and I was like, “What is happening?”
It was so strange. Afterwards, he did this impromptu Q&A with the crowd. A bunch of people rushed the stage. I could see someone from his PR team being like, “What just happened? What is he doing?” Not standard operating procedure. I thought, wow. It felt to me like Jensen Huang was just riding high on this wave, this AI wave and this incredible success that Nvidia was experiencing and the way the AI industry was growing.
Right.
But it occurred to me that he was really, really obsessive with controlling the narrative, and it reminded me of something that he’d said the first time we’d ever spoken, which was that he really admired the CEO of Adobe because he felt that the CEO of Adobe was a very good storyteller, and that he never had a pitch deck when he first pitched Nvidia as a company because he just thought it was better to tell a story.
Storytelling is so important in terms of establishing the culture of a company. He was very good at creating his own story, his own image of himself as this founder CEO who was utterly obsessed with his own company and really passionate about everything.
I guess we know where some of that passion led him.
We do indeed. It’s interesting that you talk about Jensen as a crowd favorite, because he did very much become that. He’s incredibly charismatic. He’s a great public speaker. He can really own a room. He can spin a great yarn. You describe in the cover story about Jensen, that you were “Jensen-pilled” after spending time with him, because he is so compelling.
That was interesting to me this week, in seeing how many leaders in Silicon Valley came out in support of him, despite these very, very troubling allegations, which to be clear, again, go beyond having an affair. This is beyond moral decision-making. Regardless of that, everyone from Elon Musk to Jason Calacanis came out guns blazing for Jensen.
Do you think that speaks to how revered he is in the industry, or do you think that that speaks to the fact that he is mission-critical for the industry’s ongoing growth? Are these defenses of Jensen essentially self-interested on the part of industry leaders?
I don't think they’re all self-interested. There are at least three layers to this, and one is that there are executives and lower-level tech workers who have worked for Jensen directly, and who came away from the experience with not a great taste in their mouths. They left feeling uninspired, and they actually saw a more egotistical side of him that they didn’t like, an obsessive side. There have been stories reported by other outlets about how he has sometimes berated some of his top lieutenants in front of other people. There’s almost a Dr. Jensen and Mr. Huang narrative here. He’s got two sides to him. But he’s very smart and almost can come across as sort of mensch-y. I think people really admire him.
Then I think, yes, there are people who probably own Nvidia stock, they’re industry watchers, they’re tech enthusiasts, and they see him perhaps still as a kind of our generation’s rock star who also happens to be keeping the economy afloat with his company.
So there are varying levels of interest there in terms of people who just either wish this didn’t happen, or really wish in some alternate universe he would be reinstated, which would be shocking to me at this point.
I will say WIRED had a great scoop last week, much credit to our amazing journalists, of Nvidia employees who would like to see Jensen back. There is a great deal of reverence for him, in a way that I have to admit gave me acute flashbacks to 2023, when Sam Altman was ousted at OpenAI. Very different circumstances, but yet again, a woman was installed to clean up that mess, and employees revolted and called for Sam to come back. I mean, these allegations are much more significant and serious and consequential. That said, the jury’s still out on whether Jensen makes a comeback in two weeks.
Really? You think there’s a possibility?
I think there’s a possibility.
Wow. OK. I would be very surprised. We should make a bet.
I was gonna say we should bet.
A GPU?
Oh, Lauren. I was going to say dinner the next time I’m in San Francisco.
Dinner sounds good. Let’s do it. You know what? Whoever loses the bet has to buy dinner at Proposition Chicken, which according to, was it the Daily … ?
It was the Daily Mail.
The Daily Mail reported that Proposition Chicken, which is a slightly elevated fast food chicken place in San Francisco, was being delivered to Jensen Huang’s house in Pacific Heights the other day.
OK. I’m in. Two weeks from today, we will see.
Two weeks from today.
I want to ask you lastly about ripple effects. Nvidia has invested in or bought outright plenty of AI startups. It finances a lot of the build-out happening in this industry. I have been stomping around the New York office all week screaming things like, “The global economy, the global economy!” I mean, this is much bigger than just this company, right? So what are the industry effects that we should all be watching out for from here?
What I’ve heard so far from people is that in the short term—even though we’re seeing this dip right now—there’s still just such incredible demand for Nvidia chips, and they plan everything basically 18 to 24 months out in terms of producing those chips, that I don’t think we’ll see any really serious softness in Nvidia in the short term.
But I think that the long tail of Nvidia is going to be interesting, because another CEO could come in with a totally different approach to how Nvidia spends its capital and how it also makes investments in outside companies.
Would a new CEO come in right now and make the kind of investment in CoreWeave or Perplexity, for example, that Jensen decided to? Quite possibly no. Would the new CEO come in and decide to spend so much on, let’s say, Nvidia’s healthcare division? We don’t really know. Would the new CEO come in and be as much of an open source booster as Jensen Huang had become? We don’t really know.
It’s just hard to say. The guys at Hugging Face are probably quite happy that they got in when they did.
Another thing that Jensen had set Nvidia on the path of in the past couple years was really investing in what they’re doing with CPUs as well as GPUs, which is an area that Intel and AMD are in, as well as Arm.
Was that the right path to set the company on, to over-index a little bit on CPUs for now because of the ways that the AI industry is shifting from training on high-powered GPUs to inference computing on slightly lower-powered CPUs? I think it was a smart move, but let’s see how that shakes out.
I don’t know if you remember, Katie, but back in 2008, shortly after the collapse of Lehman Brothers, a venture capitalist at Sequoia sent around a pitch deck to all of that firm’s portfolio companies that became very famous in the industry, and it’s called “RIP Good Times.”
In that pitch deck, this very prescient VC basically laid out all of the things that they wanted their portfolio companies to do, which meant saving a lot of cash. Like, this is a gird-your-loins moment. I think if we see something like that kind of mentality start to develop in Silicon Valley in the coming weeks and months, then I think that’s a very big indication that people are genuinely worried about what this Nvidia tumble means.
I am going to ask you to make one final prediction.
OK. I’m very bad at predictions, by the way, but please.
Two years ago, you said, “Huang is the man of the hour. The year. Maybe even the decade.” I would argue that that decade has been cut short, but I also think that someone like Jensen doesn’t just go quietly into the night. If he’s not reinstalled at Nvidia, and I’m wrong, and I’m buying your chicken in two weeks, where does someone like that go? Where do you expect we will see Jensen pop up in a year, in two years?
There’s a glib answer and it’s either Jensen goes to jail, or Jensen starts a podcast. I’m sure he’s hoping right now it’s the podcast outcome.
Sounds great.
Realistically, let’s say that he’s not implicated in the end result of any kind of federal investigation. And let’s say he’s not reinstated. In either case, I don’t think this is the last we’re going to hear from Jensen Huang.
